speakeroldname: Mr. R. F. SUTHERLAND (North Essex) moved :
speechtext: That that portion of the 49th rule -which limits the time for receiving petitions for private Bills, be, in accordance with the recommendation of the tenth report of the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders, suspended in reference to the petition of J. T. Schell and others on behalf of the Lake Erie and Detroit River Railway Company, praying for an Act to construct a branch line of railway, and that it be read and received forthwith.

I beg to call attention to the fact that for some years past this House has been guilty of very loose habits with regard to the time for receiving petitions for private Bills. It is provided in the British North America Act that no petition shall be presented for a private Bill after the first three weeks of the session and that no private Bill can be presented after the first four weeks of the session. That provision was made, I assume, to enable parliament to deal with its business as expeditiously as possible, and only in case of extreme urgency should the rule be suspended. The House has been now two months in session and parties desiring private legislation should have taken precaution to get that legislation before the House in due time. The rule seems now to be honoured more in the breach than in the observance; it has been so often broken that people think it is a matter of little importance to obey the rule. It is incumbent upon the right hon. gentleman who leads the House to see that the rules are closely observed, so that the business of the session may be transacted within a reasonable time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

I am forced to say that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is quite right. Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are proceeded with, I wish to call the attention of the House to a paragraph in a newspaper in regard to railway freight rates in northern and western Ontario ; and, if it is necessary to put myself in order, I will move the adjournment of the House. The question was raised in a letter addressed to the Railway Commission in regard to an increase of rates by the. Grand Trunk Railway Company, in which the company gave the excuse that they had been obliged to incur increased expenditure for maintenance and working expenses. There is no question that some additional expenditure was caused to the company by the very severe winter and the snow blockades that we have recently experienced ; but the people have suffered more than the railways from those causes. Business interests have suffered more than the railways by the detention, of goods which were ordered at Christmas and not received until March, by many perishable articles getting frozen and becoming unmerchantable while lying along the tracks of the Grand Trunk and other railways, and by winter goods being so delayed in delivery that people have had to sell them in the summer months. These are some of the ways in which the people have suffered ; yet the Grand Trunk Railway Company propose to raise their rates because they have suffered some loss. In other words, the people have no rights at all in connection with the railways of this country. The government lend to the rail- ' ways their sovereignty, so to speak, by giving them rights over private interests. In that way the railways to some extent become public highways ; and, being such, the people should have some voice in regard to their interest in these railways. I have never had any quarrel with the Grand Trunk or any other railway ; but I question the right of a railway to raise under exceptional circumstances the freight rates generally throughout the country, and make that rise practically permanent. Exceptional circumstances may have to be dealt with in an exceptional way ; but the Grand Trunk Company propose to raise the rates in Ontario simply because they have suffered loss in the abnormal circumstances which have recently existed. Have the people no rights in this matter ? Let any hon. gentleman look into the public records and see the amount of public money which the railways have received at the hands of the people, and he will come to the conclusion that the people have some rights as well as the railways. I will read from the public records to show the extent to which the people have taxed themselves in aid of railways.



The provincial government of Ontario, gave $9,708,377.69, the provincial government of Quebec gave the enormous sum of $17,561,089.08, and the municipalities of Ontario $12,000,000, and out of that $12,000,000, the Grand Trunk Railway through local roads, of which it has assumed the control, received $2,610,348.31, with in addition a loan ot $390,0(00., That is tha extent to which the people of the province of Ontario have taxed themselves through their municipalities. Taking the total mileage of railways throughout the Dominion-I am speaking generally-I find it amounts to 19,078 up to the 30th of June, 1903. During the building of that mileage, these railways received from the provincial governments an average amount equal to $1,719.77 per mile and from the municipalities $867.55, making a total average per mile of $2,587.32 for the entire mileage. That is the money which the people have spent on the railways of this country per mile, on some 19,000 miles. Before the Railway Commission, we have had the question of increased expenditure raised as a justification for increasing the freight rates. In the ' Citizen ' of yesterday, I found the following quotation from the London ' Financial Times ' regarding the appeals made to the Railway Commission to intervene in the matter of the increased freight rates over the Grand Trunk Railway :
Apparently the good people of Ontario do not realize that railways were not built in Canada solely for the purpose of providing cheap transportation for the inhabitants. Outside capital was put in for dividends, and not for philanthropy. The paper learns from a well informed source that it is very unlikely that the law authorities will intervene.
That is a very straight statement coming from a London newspaper. What authority can that paper have to say that the law authorities will not intervene 1 I would ask, is there no limit that we can set to what a railway company will do ? If a farmer should raise a bulky product, he is virtually working on shares with a railway company ; and the railway company makes a very serious mistake in charging high rates of freight on such products, because by so doing they virtually prevent the farmer from raising many jbulky products on which the companies could realize very considerable profit in the shape of freights. But so long as they impose fi eight rates which are prohibitory, so long will our farmers refuse to raise such products. The only way in which they can be induced to do so will be for the companies to charge rates that will make it possible for such products to reach the market and realize a reasonable return. It Is time that this whole question should be looked thoroughly into by parliament. Why should the Grand Trunk be allowed to take the people by the throat and say to them : we have lost money and you must make Mr. BROJVER.
up our loss. Do the men who put their money into these undertakings not run the risk of loss ? Are the people to be the only ones who stand to lose anything ? It was shown in the House a couple of years ago that while railway companies are precluded by law from raising freight rates without previously submitting these rates to the Governor in Council, yet they had invariably done so without complying with any such formality. But should they not b" compelled to submit their schedules of rates to the Railway Commission, if that is the proper authority to deal with the matter ? What right has the Grand Trunk Railway to say to the people :	we have
suffered loss and consequently are going to raise the rates ? Is there no remedy which these companies can adopt outside of taking the people by the throat ? There ought to he some remedy which can be found in the management of the road and in the way business Is being done. The companies plead increased taxation, increased price for lumber and oil, equipment, bridge building, snow blockade, etc., hut they never raise the point that there have been large increases in traffic receipts. They are careful not to point to the fact that there has been a great increase in the business of the country. If there has been an increase iu expenditure, there also has been an increase in business, hut the latter element, Mr. Hays very adroitly leaves out of the question altogether. But let him turn to the files of the ' Globe ' of a i.\ eek ago, and there he will find a glowing article showing how the railway companies were able to keep up their traffic and make money. Mr. Hays, however, carefully keeps that in the dark. Of course, with increase or business, expenses must increase. Timber. lumber, oil, coal, and all these articles, which enter into the consumption of a railway, have increased in price and Mr. Hays argues that because these things are higher, the people should pay higher freight rates, regardless of increased railway earnings. If that means anything, it means that if the railway companies find a man is making money, they are entitled to take part of his surplus. If they find a man is making a little more money than formerly, tl.ey consider they have a right to take a bigger share of his profits, hut they keep cut of sight this other fact, that if for instance, lumber Is higher at the factory, the cost of bringing the logs there, the labour, the cost of running the factory, the tic cost of putting the lumber on the cars -all these are very much increased, and the manufacturer does not get so much profit out of his lumber. Therefore, Mr. Hays lias no right to take a second slab off the sawlog, as he wants to do in this case. I have heard to-day of a man who shipped 100 barrels of apples from one of the counties west of Toronto, which were somewhat damaged in quality. The apples sold for

$100, of which the Grand Trunk got $75 end the shipper $25.	_
What about the barrels ?

The shipper lost the barrels. It is about time that something was done to bring the Grand Trunk Railway and other railway companies to a proper sense of the conditions surrounding them. \ am not opposing the. Grand Trunk Railway in particular, but speaking generally. And, Sir, it is about time for the people of Ontario to understand what the building of these railways means. If the railways, when they are built, are to take the people by the throat, the people had better be careful about the building of railways, that is all. I bring this matter up because it is important to the interests of the people. I do not wish to speak of a personal matter, but I know that local freight rates, in some cases, are away beyond what are reasonable. In many parts of the country where there is no competition they are almost prohibitory. And the local freight rates pay the losses on the through rates where there is sharp competition. There ought to be some regulation of the companies, and I hope the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads the government will see to it that the people's interests are properly protected in this matter, which is of such vital importance to every man who is carrying on business and every man who, by tillage of the soil, is increasing the products of the country.

I have to remind my hon. friend from Bundas (Mr. Broder) that parliament, only last session and after many years of agitation of the question of controlling railway rates, passed a law to create a commission for the very purpose of dealing with such questions as the hon. gentleman has brought to our attention. The commission is now in operation. I understand that their time is fully occupied, and that questions of the nature of that suggested by my hon. friend are always coming before them. It would not be advisable for the government at this time to interfere, and perhaps it would be premature also for parliament to interfere in any way until we have had some experience of the commission so that we may be able to judge what relief the people are to receive through its operation-I am sure my hon. friend will agree with me that neither the government nor parliament can do more, at this time, than give the commission a fair trial and see how far it is successful in remedying the abuses complained of.
it is the force of public opinion that largely controls railway commissions and brings to their notice grievances under which the people suffer. Now, in view of the substantial aid that the Canadian people have given towards the building of the Grand Trunk Railway and roads controlled or operated by that company, and in view of the proposal of that company, because of merely exceptional circumstances recently existing, to substantially increase their freight rates all over the country, I think it becomes absolutely necessary to draw attention to the question. Had the country not done anything to assist in building these railways, had the country not undertaken a substantial portion of the outlay involved in their construction, it might be proper to leave the matter wholly to the railway commission or the railway company ; and the Grand Trunk Railway Company might, with a certain degree of propriety, put forth the argument that they have advanced to justify their proposed increase of freight rates. I agree with the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) that it would seem that the railway companies work under a misapprehension as to the relative rights of the public and the railway corporations. I hold with Judge Black in the United States, that every railway is a highway of commerce and that every highway belongs in part to every individual who makes use of it. We are part owners of these railways. And I need only point to the fact that the franchises we have given them, the power we have given them to tax us, to take profits out of us in a hundred different ways, is an indication that we are part owners, and that we have rights-silent rights though they may be-that are too often ignored by those engaged in carrying on railway operations. The people's rights are disregarded, yet the people seem to have very little to say about the matter. So long as we assist in building railways, so long have we proprietary rights in these highways of commerce and so long should we have control to prevent them doing what is contrary to the interests of the country. I did not understand that this question was coming up at this time, and so I have not under my hand any figures showing the exact amount of money that has been given by way of federal bonus, provincial aid, municipal assistance and private contribution in land and money toward the building of the 19,000 miles of railway that we have in Canada. But, with reference to this railway that is proposing to increase its freight rates, I want to draw attention to the aid it has received for the lines that it controls. Mr. Speaker, I think the question that has been raised is one of the most important questions that we have had to consider for some time in this House, one which has attracted some attention in the past and if I am not very much mistaken will receive some consideration in the future in this House. It is rather surprising that this question, so serious as it is, should be treated so lightly by the right lion. Prime Minister, who seems to be disposed now to fall into that position of 'wait' to which he so seriously objected a year ago in reference to some other matters. There are some people who have been waiting and paying in this country. They are the farming community of Canada. We find that we have bonused railways in Canada by way of municipal, Dominion and provincial subsidies to the extent of $237,000,000, in addition to which we have granted from 57,000,000 to 62,000,000 acres of land, making about sixteen thousand dollars per mile of public aid for the total mileage in Canada, valuing the land at one dollar per acre. Now Sir, what has the farmer received for this tremendous taxation that has been imposed upon him ? We know what he has contributed towards aid to transportation in Canada. The figures are before us and surely they are large ones for a population of six or seven million people. When a community has loaned its credit and employed its powers of taxation to the extent of the figures I have just quoted, it indicates that the people are entitled to some consideration either at the hands of the government or somebody else in return for the money they have invested in this way. What are they getting for it ? It is a fact that you can ship grain or other products cheaper from Chicago to Montreal than you can from points in Ontario to Montreal. You may have a train load of grain leaving Midland and on that train there may be half a dozen cars of Canadian grain and half a dozen cars of; American grain going to the same port, going to the same destination, goipg to the same point in Canada or Europe. We have bonused these railways, built wharfs, subsidized bridges, subsidized lines of steamers in order to carry the grain from this country to Europe and what have we got out of it. We pay from ten cents to twenty cents per hundred pounds to carry Canadian grain more than is charged for foreign grain going through our country. Under these circumstances this is a question that we may spend an hour or two possibly this afternoon in discussing. It may be true that the interests of the farmers of this country do not appeal very warmly to the right hon. leader of the government. It may be that he has forgotten that there is a community in this country that have borne a heavy burden

and borne it without much grumbling or fault finding, but the time comes, and it may be only the straw, which shows which way the wind is blowing, when the people at least think they have the right to begin to consider their own welfare and I believe that in the matter of freight rates and in the matter of railways the time has arrived. Every day the Railway Committee of the House of Commons of Canada is occupied in considering blanket charters applied for by men of straw, mere brokers, as it were, gamblers in the rights and privileges that they get from this House, who have not the slightest intention of ever carrying out the undertakings with which they are identified. What is the result? These charters are traded around through the country and they are sold at anywhere from $50,000 to $500,000 acofding to the value that may be created by the opening up and peopling of the district through which the railway contemplated by the charter is designed to run. There, the burden begins. That is the beginning of the freight rate question. The price of the charter has to be paid by the freight rates which are charged in the future. On top of that comes the man who speculates in the construction of the road and who jockeys the market and saddles the road with an immense burden in order that he may make his millions out of it. The result of the whole thing is that the railway company have to impose upon the business community and the agricultural community the tremendous rates in order to carry this debt from year to year. Under the conditions that exist in this country I think we have the right to lake up a little time in the consideration of this question. When the Grand Trunk Railway Company say that because they had a difficult winter they are going to raise the freight rates in western and eastern Ontario, or in any other part of the country, or when any other railway corporation say that they propose to do the same thing, I say that they should stand in no different position from that in which any business man stands in fair competition. If he has difficulties he has to get over them. He has to pass dividends. He has to carry a profit and loss account and it is not always a profit account that he has. When some of the railway companies in Canada think that because they have had a hard winter the community must bear an extra load, it is not going to be said without a voice being raised in the House of Commons of Canada, when this House is in session and when members are supposed to be present, that we care so little about what may happen to us as a people we dare not enter our protest, forsooth, because a commission has been appointed. The commission have been appointed, I believe they have given a decision or two and I believe these decisions were cancelled by the government of the day. From the first there seems to be a Mr. POPE.
want of confidence on the part of the government as far as that commission is concerned. I ask if the Grand Trunk Railway Company carried the mails according to their contract in Ontario last winter ? They do not care a snap about their contract as far as the delivery of the mails is concerned. If it were a private party who had failed in his contract he would have to suffer. If he did not complete his contract he would be punished by being made liable for any damages which had occurred. The time has arrived when the people of Canada, who have paid for these railways, who have subsidized them to an extent that no country has ever subsidized railways are entitled to enter their protest. Under these circumstances the farmer, and every individual in this country, not only the members of this House but the taxpayers of Canada, have the right to raise their voices and express their opinion in regard to these matters more particularly in Canada than in any other country. In regard to the question of transportation in the future we have to consider very seriously the legislation of this House. If it be true that we have no hold upon these corporations, if it be true that after taxing ourselves to the extent of $300,000,000 we have no right to a voice in the matter of freight rates it is time that this parliament called a halt in regard to giving out further charters to corporations enabling them to impose burdens upon the people of Canada in future. It is time we changed our system and I believe that the time has arrived when we should give no charters, when we should issue no special privileges, but let the men who are promoting a railway get together, register themselves in a proper office to be provided for the purpose and build their road from point to point, build as many roads as they see fit and build them with their own money. Every day in the Railway Committee we see people holding up raiiways. A man applies for a charter from one point to another. We find that we have given a charter for a similar line last year or the year before. Nothing has been done. The holder of that charter comes forward and says : You are paralleling my line for 10,12, 15 or 50 miles as the case may be. I say that the corporation that will put their own money in and construct a road ought to have the privilege of paralleling any other road for which a charter has been given, and if the corporation which had the first right to build that road had not built it they should take the consequences.
The time has arrived when this parliament will be justified in considering a change in the system under which it has granted charters and privileges to special bodies of men in this Dominion. If you take the watered stock into consideration, and if you take other such matters into account, you will find that there is imposed upon the people of Canada a burden, in the paying of dividends,

that would stagger the most prosperous community on the face of the earth. The prosperity and development of our great Northwest is beyond question, but why should we shackle future generations with these heavy burdens, and why should we be told in this House that we have no right to look at the kind of shackles that are put on. I enter my protest against the Grand Trunk Company, or any other company, taking the position that because of temporary conditions they have the right to impose extraordinary burdens upon the people of Canada in the way of additional freight rates. I enter my protest against the declaration of the Prime Minister, that because there is a commission appointed we have no right to take such a matter into consideration in this House. There is nothing so important to the progress and prosperity of Canada as this very question of transportation. The mere building of a railroad will not benefit the people ; the question of how much they will have to pay to transport their products over that railroad when it is completed is the all-important consideration. We have so aided railway construction in this country that the roads have been built with comparatively little money invested by private individuals, and if we are to band over these roads to private companies without having any voice ns to the charges that are made on ihem, then it would he far better for this House to consider the purchase and the acquisition of all the railroads in Canada, so that we may try to get -some benefit out of the $230,000,000 we have expended upon them.

I do not feel it a very pleasant task to be compelled to say anything which might be calculated to accentuate the growing feeling of antagonism between the farmers and pro ducers of this country and the large railway corporations ; and that such a condition does exist no one who has his eyes and ears open can fail to recognize. I believe it is incumbent upon us in this parliament not to say anything unnecessarily that will intensify that feeling. It is only right that the people of Canada should recognize that foreign capital invested in the building of railroads has not been invested upon sentimental principles, and that railroads are not run for philanthropic purposes, hut on business principles. At the same time, at the close of a winter which has been of such an abnormally severe character, it is an inopportune time for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to come before the Railway Commission and make the proposition that they intend to increase their freight rates, to the great detriment of the farmers of this country. It is true, perhaps, that the railroads have been put to extraordinary expenses in keeping their connections open during the past winter, but there are at the same time thousands of business men throughout Ontario who have lost the profits on their business, and there are thousands of men
throughout Canada to-day who are embarrassed as a result of these same conditions. It should not be lost sight of that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, for a year before the beginning of this exceptional winter, were giving a very inferior service in Ontario, so that taking ail things into consideration a worse time could not he found in which to impose more onerous conditions on the business community. It would seem as though the Grand Trunk Railway had said : If this company loses because of abnormal climatic conditions, or if the Ontario government think it well to increase taxation on railways, we will take good care that we shall not lose anyway, but that we will make -the public pay for it in the shape of increased freight rates. Canada has granted more aid in the shape of money and land grants for the development of railway communication than has a-ny other country in the world. The people of this country have to a large extent taxed themselves for the building of these roads, and those who invested their private capital in the enterprise should recognize that if exceptional conditions arise, and if their profits are reduced, they have to take their chances on that score. If the shareholders have had their dividends reduced, it must not be forgotten also that the farmers of Ontario have been unable to get their products to the market, and that the business men though being unable to transact business, have suffered corresponding losses.
I would not like to see the feeling of antagonism that exists between the railway corporations and the farmers of this eoun-trv accentuated more than- it is at present. There is a marked and growing feeling today that we are not a self-governing people, but that the country is largely dominated by great railway corporations-that it is being practically sold to them and governed by them. This is an unhappy state of things, and it would be well if to some extent it could be ameliorated. It would be well if the producers would always recognize the fact that money is invested in railway corporations in order to earn dividends, and that that money is not always invested by people of wealth who have abundance and can afford to lose, but that in many cases it is the small capital of people in humble circumstances. Therefore, it is reasonable that over a series of years there should be a fair return for the money invested in the railways of the country ; but for the railway corporations to take advantage of an exceptional season to make a permanent rise of rates is something that will be keenly resented by the people, in view of the liberal grants which they have made in land and in other ways in aid of these railways. There should be some consideration of this by the railway companies themselves. The people of this country are paying a very large share of the cost not only of building these roads, but of maintaining them ;

and the railway companies should not have the power to dominate so completely the material interests of the country as practically to put a price on all the products of the country. So that no longer can a man say that he can raise any particular article at a profit, but it is for the railway companies to say whether there shall be any profit left to him or not. This is against the material interests not only of one class of our people, but of the country at large, and therefore it is important that the whole matter should have full and fair consideration in the House and before the country.

Mr. Speaker, I do not take up much of the time of this House, but I feel it my duty to have something to say on this important question. I was not one of those who believed that the appointment of a railway commission was going to be in the interest of the general public. X looked upon it as a hiding place for any government that might be in power. It is like farming out a job ; the government can hide behind tlie commission. I have not yet seen any benefit from it. Although I believe it has given one or two decisions, the government has overruled them. I understand that after the commission gives a decision on any question, it has then to come before the government, which is to say whether it will stand or not. Now, it is an easy matter for a railway corporation or railway officials to come and see this commission privately, compared with seeing the government or the House of Commons, composed of 214 members. Though I was not one of those who believed in the appointment of a railway commission, I notice that it has had one result. We do not need a Minister of Railways any more. Since its appointment he has not appeared in this House, and the only thing he has done in connection with railway matters has been to sign the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific. He has not said a word on the Bill so far, but is leaving to the other members of the government all the explanations of the contract to which he put his signature. The railway companies talk about the great losses they have sustained during the past winter from snow blockades and other things ; but the people throughout the country have suffered great loss and inconvenience as well as the railways. All we could do was to bear our troubles and say nothing. But we think 'it is unjust for the railways to impose on the people extra freight charges in order that they themselves may be at no loss. I do not usually growl at the railways ; but I wish to state that during the past winter I sold a number of young cattle. By an arrangement made with the railways some years ago, all the registered stock are carried at half rates. The cattle are snpposed to be of a certain weight according to their age. An animal which is one day over two years old will be charged just double what a Mr. RICHARDSON.
two years' old animal will be. I sold eight head of cattle. The oldest one was three months short of being a year old. I could not get a car at my station, either on the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Pacific Railway, to take those calves away until the oldest one became two years old. The result was that I had to pay twice as high a freight charge as I would have had to pay had I got the accommodation at the time they were sold. It cost me $21 to provide for the feeding of these cattle during the time they had to wait for railway accommodation. If this government will stand by and let the railway corporations raise the freight rates as they please, and then go and settle the matter with the three commissioners whom the government have appointed, the people will not be satisfied. I believe this is the thin edge of the wedge ; and if the Grand Trunk is allowed to raise the freight rates, there will be nothing to hinder the Canadian Pacific Railway and all the other railroads in the country from doing the same. The railways do not fight against each other, even at competing points. What we call competition is not competition at all. The railways charge the same rate from competing points, and we have only the choice of two lines. If the government would settle this matter in the interest of the whole public, instead of leaving it in the hands of three commissioners, it would be better for the country at large. I sympathize with the railways in the trouble and expense to which they have been put in struggling with snow blockades during the past winter ; but the farmers throughout the country have had to spend their own money in clearing the highways. They have had to stand that loss, and why should not the railways stand their losses ? They have their good times as well as their bad times, just as the farmers have ; but the farmers have no means of making anybody pay their losses but themselves.
I think that the government should act right away and say to these companies : we will fix your rates of freight, you are not in a position to say to the people that because you have lost money the people must reimburse you. What I would like to know is whether railway companies have the right to take this position, that because they have lost money during the winter, they will raise their freight rates during the summer, and thus make the public pay their loss. If there ever was an argument which convinced me that the sooner we have government owned railroads the better, it is the stand taken by this railway company. I hope that the government will not wait until the railway commission deals with the matter , but wrill take steps to have the commission deal with it right away, in order that the people may get fair play.

This is a subject, Mr. Speaker, that

comes very close home to the general public, and while I have no desire to make a speech, I wish to submit a few facts to the attention of the House.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Louder.

I am suffering from a cold and cannot yell. If hon. gentlemen will keep still and pay a litle attention, they will hear what I have to say. I was sorry to see the Prime . Minister and the Postmaster General talking and laughing when this serious matter was up before the House. It may be very nice for them to talk and laugh when the money of the people is being taken out of the people's pockets. That of course does not concern them. As long as they are in office and get their salaries and enjoy a good time, they care little who is bled. But the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) I know will not laugh, because in times gone by. when the Conservative party was in office, he was wont to indulge in a very mournful wail over the farmers being bled white. 1 often wonder how that hon. gentleman feels now7. But I just want to draw7 to his attention and that of the right hon. the Prime Minister, the present condition of things, and to ask them why they should want us to wait until we see what the commission will do. Why, only last year, when introducing the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill, with such a flourish of trumpets, we were told by the right hon. gentleman that time w7ould not w7ait and that every moment that w7as lost was lost for ever. But now he tells us to wait and see what the Railway Commission will do. But I say that not a moment should be lost in urging the Railway Commission to prevent the Grand Trunk Railway putting this iniquitous proposition of theirs into effect. I have no feeling against the' Grand Trunk Railway or any other railway. I have been in this House many years and have aided by my voice and vote the construction of many railways, but after these roads are constructed, we do not want to be oppressed-, as we have been, by these railway companies which we have bonused, not only by provincial and Dominion subsidies, but also by municipal grants, which we have paid by direct taxation. What is the position in which we are? We are told by the Grand Trunk Railway that because they have had a hard winter, they must make the farmers pay for it. But have we not all had a hard winter ? Let me tell those people from the Northwest who are complaining about the difficulty of getting coal in that section, that we were in the same position in Ontario on the main line of the Grand Trunk Railway. For weeks and almost months our people could not get in or out over these roads, which we had paid for out of our own pockets. If
the Prime Minister has not time to deal with this matter, I know that the Minister -of Trade and Commerce has plenty of time on his hands. We are paying a large sum to that hon. gentleman for his cab hire, and if he cannot walk, he can drive to that commission and see that this matter is attended to. Let me draw to his attention the fact that these hundred barrels of apples, which were spoken about to-day, v ere sent from the village of Hastings, in the north part of the county which I have the honour to represent. They were sent over a road to which the peoplejraid large bonuses by direct taxation, and that company charged 75 cents a barrel for bringing these apples from Hastings down to Ottawa. I sent some apples on commission to Great Britain this year, and the freight to that country was only $1 per barrel That surely is a matter to which we should give a little attention. This whole question is one of great importance to the people, and the Ministers would do far better to give it their serious attention instead of allowing members on their side to fritter away the time of the House talking on the same subjects and repeating the same speeches, and in listening to which my head has grown gray. Apparently the Minister of Trade and Commerce has no time to give any attention to a subject which so closely interests the farmers, with whom in the olden days he used to sympathize so deeply. But of course, talk is cheap, and once in office, we find these people, who were so vociferous in opposition, not willing to give the slightest heed to the principles or policies they then advocated and quite content to remain silent in their seats while the farmers are being bled, not only by this extravagant government, but also by these railway companies which we have so largely bonused. There is another point, and one w7hich I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher). We are advised from Great Britain that our people's shipments to that country arrive in a bad condition. To w7hat is that due ? In the village of Brighton, W7here there is the largest storage accommodation in the Dominion, shippers have been so handicapped by the fact that they could not get cars properly heated to carry their fruit, that they had to take anything the Grand Trunk Railway would stnd them. Consequently the apples got frozen and arrived in poor condition. That was not due to any fault on the part of the farmers, but because the railway company did not provide the proper facilities to carry the fruit to market. If the Minister of Agriculture had paid less attention to fattening chickens and more to the carriage of freight, Hhat difficulty might have been avoided. If the Prime Minister would take this matter into serious consideration and consult with the Minister of Trade and Commerce, something might

b ; done. Then we have this other injustice inflicted on Canadians. The same road which will carry a Yankee from the state of Michigan to New York at the rate of two cents a mile will charge a Canadian three cents a mile, although that company has been aided by Canada to the extent of from $75,000,000 to $100,000,000. It is an insult to the Canadian people to say that a railway chartered by them and aided by them to such an enormous extent should be allowed to treat our people with such unjust discrimination.
I want to-impress that upon the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has not much else to do in that place that he spoke of as a sinecure before he got into it. Now that he has plenty of time, he ought to pay attention to this matter. And I am sure that, now that the case is brought to his attention, he will avail himself of the opportunity to do something to earn his money.

Living, as I do, on one of the branch lines of the Grand Trunk Railway in western Ontario, I have good reason in my own experience to know that the hon. member for Dundas (Mr. Broder) and other hon. members who have spoken have good ground for the criticisms they have directed against that company. We not only have to pay high freight rates, but we have great difficulty in getting cars in reasonable time. We suffer from this difficulty now, but the same difficulty existed even last year, before the snow blockade. Then, the time-tables on these branch lines are a very poor guide as to when the trains will come along. It is quite a usual thing for trains to be an hour or an hour and a half late. I am not speaking of freight or mixed trains, but what are called express or mail trains. Occasionally a train will be on time, and so the public are obliged always to be at the station at the hour given in the time table, and very much valuable time is wasted in this way. These causes of annoyance have been frequently brought to the attention of the company, but, though there has been some temporary improvement it has never continued for a very long time.

I am like the hon. member for Cardwell (Mr. Johnston), I had great faith in the Railway Commission, I have been advocating the establishment of a court at which the farmers could plead their grievances and have them redressed. And now the government have appointed a railway commission and we are expecting great things from it. Perhaps we are expecting too much. The commission will have to be governed by the Railway Act. If the Act gives them no power to settle a question of freight rates between the railway companies and the producers and consumers, we might as well Mr. COCHRANE.
have no commision. It seems to me, however, that they have power to say what shall be a maximum rate. If that power is not conferred by the law then we had better change the law at once. It seems 1o me that this is a very inopportune time for the Grand Trunk Railway Company to-fail foul of the people of Canada, just at a time when they are asking so many privileges from the government-but they have not got them yet. I suppose that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is connected with this Grand Trunk Pacific, and that it is on behalf of the Grand Trunk that these privileges are being asked. We are to give them a transcontinental road for fifty years to operate without let or hindrance. I think they should think twice before they impose heavier taxes upon the farmers of this country as they seem to intend doing. They are going to levy a higher rate( both ways upon the stuff they carry. That is what I understood from what was stated by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Broder) who introduced this question. If they are allowed to do that, what does it mean ? It means this : that it will not only reduce the price of what we have to sell but it will increase the price of what we have to buy. And the necessary effect of that is that it will reduce the value of our land. These men are masters of the situation. By a stroke of the pen, they can say what we shall pay for what we buy and what we shall receive for our labour. It is time that this condition was changed. I do not think that the government have any power to act at once under the circumstances. I am not one of those therefore who shout at the government to jump up at once and do something. If the Railway Commission has power to settle this difficulty, let them settle it; if not, let us pass a law that will give that power. We are apt to boast and to sing very loudly 'Britons never shall be slaves,' But we are all slaves to the railway corporation, and we are going to be greater slaves, and slaves for all time, if you hand over the Transcontinental Railway to the Grand Trunk. We shall be slaves for fifty years anyway, and that is as long as I am likely to live. I know that this is not the time to discuss the Transcontinental Railway. But the question is whether these people have the right to place these heavy taxes on the farmers and not let them have a word to say about it. The first tiling the railway commission ought to do is to find out what it costs to carry a ton of freight or a passenger a hundred miles. If they do not know that now, the best thing they can do is to figure it out. Then, they would have some basis to go upon. At present, we are groping in the dark. We have been advertising Canada for a number of days in this House as a country that is in a deplorable state in winter. We abused Kipling like everything because he called our

country. ' Our Lady of the Snows.' But we go on so much further than anything he said that we are apt to prove that our country is Our Lady of the Frost as well as Our Lady of the Snows. We do not want to say too much about these things. We do not want to let a railway company think that because they get stalled for a few days in winter they are to take that as an excuse for laying heavier burdens upon the producers and consumers. I remember reading a story not long ago-and you know I very seldom tell stories-of how one of the magnates in the United States was petitioned for a grant to the University of Chicago. He asked how much was required, and was told that half a million or so, would set the institution on a proper basis. He wrote his cheque and then turned to his clerk and said, ' Put up coal oil two cents a gallon.' In a month he had his money back from the consumers of coal oil. That is about the way these railway companies are going to do with us-use the extra expense of an unusually severe winter as an excuse for laying burdens upon us out of all proportion to the cost. I do not want to make a speech but only to enter my protest, not against the position of the government, but against any monopolists in this country being allowed to treat people as the railways are treating us today.

I understand the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who leads the House to say that this is not an opportune time to bring up this matter and endeavour to secure a remedy. He seems to think that this is a time for us to pause, to consider, to delay, to deliberate. This is the time when the hon. gentleman would have us say : Tomorrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow. It is a time when we are not to be in any hurry, a time when we are to let matters drift as they will, leaving the farmers in the meantime, to suffer as they may. I understand that the right hon. gentleman says that the remedying of this grievance should be left to the Railway Commission.
Either the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) knows this or he does not know it. If he understands it at all he is not giving us the best conclusion he could arrive at. The Railway Commission cannot remedy all the grievances of which the people are complaining. I may say here that I have not that abiding faith in the Commission which the right hon. gentleman seems to have. I presume the right hon. gentleman is aware, being the leader of a great business government, that there are other grievances besides rates of which the people are complaining, that for many months past, if not for years, the question of not having adequate accommodation and reasonable facilities for the transportation for the products of this country from point to point, has been as serious as the question of rates. It is important for the government to know that great as the congestion is in the west, crying as is the need for additional facilities for transporting the produce of the west, great and immediate as is the need of a transcontinental railway, equally great is the need, in the older portions of Ontario, of having the Grand Trunk so equipped that it can with reasonable facility carry the produce of old Canada from place to place and from port to port. I do not know whether the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is aware that the Grand Trunk Railway which has now been in operation for more than half a century having absorbed the Great Western and other of the old railways of Canada is today very poorly equipped for the transportation of the produce of Canada. Its equipment is on a par with that of the Intercolonial although the Intercolonial Railway is now like an old song, they are going to throw it away ; it has never been, according to the government, a railway of any importance, and they are going to side-track it. The Grand Trunk Company which is supposed to be able to serve every city and town in old Ontario and Quebec and to a large extent in the maritime provinces has only the same equipment as we have on the Intercolonial Railway. Of engines the Grand; Trunk has 22 to the 100 miles ; the Intercolonial has 21 to the 100 miles. Of freight cars the Grand Trunk has 775 to the 100 miles, and the Intercolonial 774 to the 100 miles. Now what is the remedy the right hon. gentleman tells the people of Canada he is going to apply to this ? He says that when we come to have the Railway Commission running smoothly-and I do not know when that is going to be, it did not start off very smoothly in the matter of telephones- we will have these matters adjusted. We cannot have these matters adjusted by the Railway Commission ; the remedy was for the government, when the Grand Trunk came to them and said they were going to open up the west, to have said :	We want
as a guarantee for the services you are to render in the new land something to show that you have carried out what is necessary in the old territory which you occupied before ; we want you to give some guarantee, aye, and to implement it if you will, that you will give adequate facilities for the-transportation of the grain over the territory you already occupy before we open up a new territory for you at vast expense to the people of Canada. The government had the opportunity to exercise that control ; to-a large extent, they have it yet. This transcontinental railway scheme is not yet consummated, and it is becoming more difficult of consummation every day. The government I know are hesitating now ; they do not know exactly what the next move is to be. I urge upon the government to take-

this matter In hand, to be practical business men and now when they have the opportunity I ask the right lion, gentleman and his colleagues to pause, to consider, to delay, to deliberate and let the result of it be that we will have a better bargaiu for the people of Canada, particularly in the matter we are discussing this afternoon.
There is another matter that is not entirely under the control of the Railway Commission, that is the question of accidents.

speechtext: Order. I think my hon. friend should coniine himself to the question of freight rates which has been brought up by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Broder).

I understand that the adjournment was moved on the question of railways but as I am not particularly anxious to speak on the question of accidents I shall not insist; but at the same time I would be very glad to have your ruling, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: The question as I understood it was a question of freight rates purely and simply, and I think that it would perhaps be better if the hon. gentleman would limit himself to that subject.
The same point was raised only a few days ago and Mr. Deputy Speaker moved exactly to the contrary ?
Take your choice.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that there is one very important point that has not been dealt with in this discussion this afternoon. One of the reasons that the general manager of the Grand Trunk Railway Company gave for raising the rates of freights was that the Grand Trunk Railway Company have been compelled to pay $230,709 in taxes or something like $75,000 more than they were held to pay the previous year. This is the increase according to the figures as given in the ' Globe ' of Saturday last. AVe have not stopped to consider the question as to whether the Ontario government were justified in passing the Act imposing heavier taxes on the Grand Trunk Railway Company

or upon any other company. The Grand Trunk Railway Company complain because they own the only double tracked road in Ontario or in the Dominion of Canada. It is true that the Michigan Central is partially double tracked, but the Grand Trunk Railway Company, I understand, suffer more by reason of this than any other line of railway. Their double track costs per mile .$40 taxation, and that is what they complain of as being particularly hard on them. The Ontario government have the right to impose these taxes but the right to control railways has been taken out of the hands of the provincial governments and placed in the hands of the Dominion government. The Ontario government have placed this tax upon the railway companies in Ontario and I want to draw the attention of the House to the fact that had it not been for the enormous extravagance of the Ontario government many of the taxes which they have imposed on the people would not be necessary. They have taxed the living and they are taxing the dead. They are taxing every professional gentleman in the province, they are placing taxes upon every insurance company anil bank in the province, they are placing taxes wherever they can in order to raise funds to meet the extravagant expenditure they are making from year to year. It must be admitted that where a government impose taxes unnecessarily, whether it be on insurance companies, railway companies, or upon any other line of business carried on in any province, these companies must of necessity impose larger rates on the public in order to meet this increased taxation. The Ontario legislature voted not long ago $2,000,000 to the Consolidated Lake Superior Company and took the Algoma Central Railway as security, a road that they themselves furnished the money and'gave the lands to build, taking as security au institution that they themselves brought into existence. The voting of this sum of money was quite unnecessary and quite uncalled for. I wish to draw the attention of the government to the fact that when the Hon. G. W. Ross became premier of the province of Ontario he made a speech at Whitby during the course of which he made this statement:
The Ontario government has nothing to do with the control of railways. The control of railways has been taken from us. I was in the House of Commons when that change was made, and I regret that it was made. We want to get into the British market, and I pledge my word as leader of the government that the Ontario government will lend all the assistance in its power to encourage the Dominion government in providing quick and cheap transportation for our produce to England. The Dominion government cannot afford to turn a deaf ear to our representatives in the Ontario legislature. When the Ontario legislature asks they must move, because more than one-half of the influence of this country lies in Ontario. It shall be my early duty to see if there cannot be a
reduction of freights to ocean ports on agricultural products.
I would like to ask the right hon. leader of the government if he has ever been petitioned by the Ontario government, or if the leader of the Ontario government has ever interceded on behalf of the farmers of the province of Ontario in order to secure cheap transportation. But, what do we find the premier of Ontario doing in the following session after he had made the statement at Whitby ? The following motion was moved by a gentleman who represented one of the ridings of the city of Toronto-Mr. Crawford :
That in the opinion of this House it is the duty of tile provincial government to, without delay, urge upon the government of Canada, the necessity of taking steps to obtain for the people of this province, cheaper rates for the transportation of agricultural products.
Would it surprise the right hon. leader of the government if I told him that not only Mr. Ross but every one of his followers voted against that resolution asking for cheaper transportation ? I am afraid that this is in line with- some of the professions made by hon. gentlemen opposite. These hon. gentlemen make great professions in the country but when resolutions are brought into the House they vote against the principles which they have proclaimed outside. I would like further to state that upon referring to the General Railway Act I find in section 255 the following under the head of ' freight classification ' :
The tariffs of tolls for freight traffic shall be subject to and governed by that classification which the board may prescribe or authorize.
I find further in section 250 :
All tariff by-laws and tariffs of tolls shall be in such form, size and style, and give such information, particulars and details, as the board may, by regulation, or in any case, prescribe.
In section 257 I find the following :
The board may disallow any tariff or any portion thereof which it considers to be unjust or unreasonable.
If that be true and if this matter is submitted to the commission, then, I take it that if the commission find that the rates imposed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company are exorbitant or unreasonable they have the power to refuse to sanction these increased rates in the matter of freight. But, I take it that if this matter is brought before the commissioners they will weigh well and carefully the nature of the obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. If the obligations of the Grand Trunk are so and so by reason of certain provincial legislation, whether it he by the Ontario government or any other government in this Dominion, and if they have been imposed through no fault of the Grand Trunk Company, then, the commissioners must take

into account the question as to whether the reasons for increasing the rates were good and sufficient and if they are the Grand Trunk	Railway	Company	will	be	justified in charging the rates which they have charged. If that cannot be proved	then I	take it	that	it	will
be their duty to disallow the rates imposed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. As members of this House I think it is our duty to point out the weakness of the action of the provincial government in imposing obligations on railways that we in this parliament have the right to control and to point out that the provincial government should exercise greater economy in the administration of the affairs of that province and thus remove any reason for imposing unnecessary taxes on the Grand Trunk Railway Company or any other railway company in this country. '
Personally, I am in favour of having as low freight rates as possible on the Grand Trunk or any other railway. I believe that one cent more paid for transportation is a cent out of the pockets of the farmers of this country, and that a cent saved on transportation is a cent earned by the farmers. If the government of Ontario had exercised economy and had not increased the expenditure from $3,000,000 to nearly $6,000,000, they would not to-day find it necessary to impose this taxation. And .let me point out to the right hon. the Prime Minister that when he is proposing legislation which will entail vast expenditure, let him remember that every burden he imposes upon the people will interfere with the welfare and prosperity of Canada.
Motion (Mr. Broder) to adjourn negatived.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Before we proceed, I wish to say a word with regard to a document which has been quoted from by members on this side of the House, and which is a report of the minutes of proceedings of the ordinary general half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of the -Grand Trunk Railway Company, held at the Terminus Hotel, Cannon street, London, E.C., on Tuesday, the 8th of March, 1904. This report has been attacked from the other side of the House by more than one speaker. In fact, one bon. gentleman described it as a fabricated document, and said that it was a fake report. That was the description given of it by a very prominent speaker on the other side. It is to all intents and purposes the same as the report in the ' Railway News,' but there are some minor differences ; the speeches of some of the shareholders are reported fully in this document, whereas they Mr. INGRAM.	.
are not reported in the ' Railway News.' As these insinuations have been made against the correctness of this document, I have thought it right to have it verified, and I now have a declaration, having all the sanctity of an oath, from the gentleman who attended the meeting and prepared the report. The declaration is as follows :
I, James Watson Mills, of 13 Cheverton Road, Hornsey Lane, in the county of London, shorthand writer and reporter, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows
On the 8th March, 1904, I attended the ordinary general half-yearly meeting of shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, Canada, and the printed report hereto annexed marked ' A ' with the red ink alterations initialled by me is a true report of the proceedings of such meeting, and I hereby verify the correctness thereof to the best of my belief.
And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing the same to be true and by virtue of the provisions of the ' Statutory Declarations Act. 1835.'
Declared at St. Lawrence House, Trump Street, in the city of London, the 28th day of April, 1904.
Before me,-
(Sgd.) W. W. Hortin,
A commissioner for oaths.
(Signed) JAMES W. MILLS.
I should say that the alterations which are made in this printed document are, I think, not material,, except so far as one is concerned. That error was obvious, and it was corrected in the copies of this document which some weeks ago I sent across the floor to hon. gentlemen opposite. I have prepared a copy of this document exactly as it has been verified by Mr. Mills, and I will be glad to place it in the possession of my hon. friends on the other side.
I think it would have been well if we on this side of the House had been furnished with copies of what is called the official report of the meeting of shareholders of the Grand Trunk Company, which has been largely quoted from by gentlemen on the other side. We have not had the courtesy of being furnished with that report, but I have procured a copy. It does not purport to contain the speeches in full, but there is one important statement in it which it might be well to bring to the attention of the House. In the special report of directors to the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, bearing date the 20th day of February, 1904, which was considered at that meeting, and which has as an appendix the fwo agreements-although I think there are some few typographical or clerical errors in the copies of the agreement annexed-in that report Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson states most distinctly what was afterwards stated in the speech of himself and of other directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. One paragraph of the report previously sent out and read to the shareholders on that occasion is this :

It should be mentioned that in consideration of the guarantees and other assistance given to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, the Grand Trunk Railway Company are to receive the whole of the $25,000,000 of common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company.
We have proposed several amendments to the Bill, and the Minister of Justice suggested that we should give these to him, in order that he might furnish to us a written statement of the reasons on account of which he might not see fit to agree if he did not agree. I have not received from the Minister of Justice any statement of reasons, although I believe that my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has a letter from the Minister of Justice stating that as to certain of these proposed amendments the government does not see its way clear to assent. We are, therefore, not very much further along than we were before we gave these amendments to my hon. friend. I observe in a recently established organ of the government the assertion that this was designed as a ' trap.' Well, I do not suppose there is anything in that, but still it may be well that these arrangements made across the floor of the House would be carried out perhaps a little more strictly in the line of what was intended. I am not much afraid of any trap we may have been led into, although it is asserted in this organ of the government that this was a trap or intended as a trap, and that a very great stroke of strategic genius has been performed by the government in inducing us to hand over these amendments.
I do not regret giving the government time to consider them ; I would do so again ; but it is not perhaps in very good taste, after a courtesy a little out of the ordinary course has been accorded by this side of the House, for organs of the government, recently established in the province of Quebec, and speaking for the government, to make these assertions in regard to gentlemen on this side of the House.

That section 1 of the Bill be amended by adding thereto the following as subclause (2) :-
(2.) It is hereby declared that the intent and meaning of the agreement, a copy of which forms the schedule to the National Transcontinental Railway Act, was, and as modified by the supplementary agreement, a copy of which forms a schedule to this Act, is, that the rolling stock in the twenty-second clause of the said original agreement mentioned, as the first equipment, shall be so acquired by the Pacific Company that an absolute and indefeasible interest therein shall vest In the said company subject only to the several mortgages referred to in clause thirty-five of the agreement, and free from any prior charge, rent, or interest whatsoever, whether as working expenditure or otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that this amendment is intended to give effect to the objection raised in the course of the debate on the Bill introduced last year. My hon. friend argued that the rolling stock might be acquired under a title which would enable the company to hand it over to ns subject to a prior lien. In addition to that, my hon. friend has argued that under the provisions of the Railway Act at the time the Bill was introduced, this rolling stock would be subject to a prior lien in respect oi any penalty that had been incurred and also in respect of working expenses. That, I believe, was the argument of the hon. member for Hamilton the other day.
Mr. BARKER, My argument was this, that if the rolling stock be acquired subject to a 'rental, that rental would be a portion of the working Expenses, and would rank ahead of the mortgage.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My argument is that under the contract as, we have it, the rolling stock must be held in absolute ownership, free from any claims or liens, before it can he considered as having been held according to the terms of the contract.

That brings us hack to the original argument. What we have contended throughout is that in the 22nd clause of the original agreement there are no words which even by implication call for the acquisition of the rolling stock free from any rent charge. All that the clause provides is that the company shall equip the road with $20,000,000 of rolling stock. W7e tried last year to get the Minister of Justice to accept a suggestion that words should be included in that clause expressly stating that the rolling stock should he acquired and paid for, so that there should he no doubt upon that subject. We contend that the word ' equip ' would he sufficiently satisfied by putting the rolling stock on the road under any conditions whatever, whether as rented or hired, or purchased on Mr. FITZPATRICK.
time, with a large charge for the purchase money on it, or purchased and paid for. Some hon. gentlemen contended that because section 85 of the agreement required the company to give a first mortgage on all the property, including the equipment, that in itself showed that the rolling stock must be owned absolutely.
I referred to the provisions of the Railway Act to show that the giving of a first mortgage does not necessarily mean that the property must he owned absolutely by the company. I referred also to the 18th section of the Act of last session incorporating the Grand Trunk Pacific, which enabled the Grand Trunk Pacific to give this first mortgage that is called for in clause 35 of the agreement. In that section there is provision made for giving a first mortgage, subject to the conditio is of section 94 of the then General Railway A ct. When you turn to section 94, you find that the first mortgage to be given by any railway company is subject to the working expenditure ; and when you turn to the definition of working expenditure, you find that it includes the rent of rolling stock. In addition to that you find that clause 14 of the original agreement-the one referring to the rolling stock equipment for the eastern division-expressly refers to rent of the rolling stock in connection with that * very equipment. Under these circumstances what did we say ? We said that you could have removed all doubt on the question by simply using the words ' acquire and pay for.' We urged that again and again last year. The answer then given was, first, it .was considered clear that there must be an acquisition free from any charge, because a first mortgage upon the property must be given under clause 35, and second that the agreement had been settled with the Grand Trunk Railway and could not be altered. Since then that agreement was cast aside by the Grand Trunk Railway, who refused to confirm if. Subsequently negotiations took place between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway, resulting in this supplementary contract, which alters the original contract in may particulars. Yet, although this question of the rolling stock, take what ever view you like, must he a doubtful one, the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches did not take advantage of their opportunity to remove any doubt but left it just as it was. This is not a trifling question, but an exceedingly important one from two points of view. First of all, as regards the $5,000,000 of rolling stock for the equipment of the eastern division, the result of any rent charge or interest on that rolling stock is that the government will not obtain as their security tor *the preformance by the Grand Trunk Pacific of the conditions of the lease a first mortgage on that $5,000,000 of property, [DOT]which is the only security the government have got, first and last, for the performance
of the covenants of the Grand Trunk Pacific ; and moreover the interest or rent upon the rolling stock will be ahead of our rental under the lease. Not only is that the case with regard to thjj eastern division, but instead of having a first mortgage on the western division to secure the bonds we guarantee, we have $15,000,000 of an encum-biance placed prior to these bonds, because if the $20,000,000 of rolling stock are not acquired by clear and absolute title free from rent, the working expenditure of the western division will include the rental of three-fourths of that rolling stock, and be ahead of our mortgage. That is the result of leaving this question where it is. I do not c-are, for my part, as a matter of business, whether the view taken by the Minister of Justice be more or less arguable than ours, but I say it is absurd, having regard to the difference of opinion on this point having regard to the fact that the hon! gentleman has had to obtain opinions of counsel upon it, that it should have been left in a state of uncertainty, when all doubt might have been removed by a few words. That is the position I take, and we are .iustified in finding fault with the government that in a matter of such moment- the question of whether $20,000,000 obligation shall be ahead of our rent and oui mortgage should be left open to a difference of opinion, as a question perhaps to be settled by the courts, when it could have been settled by the insertion of two or three words in the supplementary contract I therefore think, as it is not yet too late as we are yet considering the advisability of validating this contract, we should not lose this opportunity to declare that this contract means what hon. gentlemen opposite have all along said it does, but which Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson says it does not mean. Wily should the government hesitate to declare in this Act that the contract means what they themselves say it does ? The non.. Minister of Justice says we hav;e nothing to do with the opinion of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson. Nevertheless why should we not declare what our view is, and let that be the law, and then there will be no question for litigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know that any good purpose would be served by my going over again the argument I offered seme time ago. The contract provides for an absolute obligation on the part of the company to give us a title, absolutely free to this property, so that we will be able to secure a first mortgage upon it. Mv hon friend says that the $5,000,000 of rolling stock is the only security we shall have for the working of the eastern division. He has entirely overlooked clause 25 which provides :
The said lease shall also contain such other covenants and provisions, including proper indemnity to the government in respect of the working of the railway as may he deemed necessary by the government to secure the proper carrying out of this agreement.
I said you would have the covenant of the Grand Trunk Pacific.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: And we will have the indemnity they will be obliged to give us for the working of the railway.
It is the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know that indemnity is the same thing as covenant. Perhaps it is. I have never looked upon it as the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: What importance dees the hon. gentleman attach to it ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Very considerable. They can indemnify us against any breach of the agreement in the working of the railway. They must give us indemnity to the effect that they will properly work this railway, the form of indemnity to be determined at the time -the contract is made. Mith reference to the working expenditure raking precedence over the lien of the government let me draw the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that section 94 of the Railway Act is not the section that applies in this case. The question is whether, under section 35 they can fail to give us a first lien on the property. They undertake to give us such a lien. As I say the right is not to be exercised under section 94 of the Railway Act, but under section 3o of the agreement. It seems to me that there is all the difference in the world.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I must confess that T do not quite understand the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Fitzpatrick's) argument. I do not understand what value he gives to the word ' indemnity.' In the preparation of legal documents, so far as I have had experience, an indemnity is created by a covenant. The hon. gentleman seems to find some extraordinary difference between ' indemnity ' and ' covenant.' As I say, indemnity is usually created by covenant and would be, I suppose, in this ease. I supposed at first that he meant that the -word 'indemnity' involved security. If that was the effect of his argument I could understand it. But the hon. gentleman does not put that forward. So. it is reduced, as my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) says to the covenant of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and nothing more. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fitzpatrick) relies altogether on section 35. But this must be construed in connection with section 14. In the argument, of the Minister of Justice and in the opinions which have been given by the Deputy Minister of Justice and by Mr. Shepley, paragraph 14 of the contract is absolutely ignored. Yet, it must be read in connection with paragraph 35. Now, paragraph 14 says distinctly that the words ' working expendi-

If that is not a distinct recognition ot the ii<=ht of the company to equip the eastern division by means of rolling stock on hire, I do not Know what expression would convey that idea. Mr. Shepley, in his argument, says that he does not see how, in view ot the conditions in the contract to which his telegram refers, it is possible to argue that the hiring of rolling stock would be an equipment within the meaning of thereon-tract. The use of these words by Mr. Shep-ley would indicate clearly that his attention had not been directed to clause 14 of the agreement.
