forward by the minister. But if their mter-i pretation of the contract is the same as that of the minister, and if it is m the public interest that that should be made clear, i think there is every reason why the change should be made. Different men may be at the head of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the future, or there may be a different administration in power. it is desirable, in view of these contingencies of the future to remove all possible doubt and make the meaning absolutely plain. I think that, under the circumstances, the amendment of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is a reasonable one, and one which the government in all fairness, and in the public interest should adopt.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It seems to me that the hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) when he takes that position has perhaps not fully considered all its bearings. He says, as I understand'his argument, that the words :
As part of the equipment of the said eastern division.
do not relate to the first equipment, but to some subsequent equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Any additional equipment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes. Has my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) fully considered the language of section 35 when he takes that stand ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think so ; I tried to consider everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Let us look for a moment at the wording of that clause :
A mortgage which shall be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property, tolls, rights and franchises of the company, including all equipment and property to he thereafter acquired by the company.
That carries my hon. friend too far.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It certainly does, and I will show you how in a very few moments. He must admit that section 14 contemplates that the equipment, a portion of the equipment at least of the eastern division, a portion of some of the equipment, either the first or a subsequent equipment, shall be acquired by hiring by the company. If he does not admit that, I do not know what office those words serve ; they do not serve any office if they do not mean that. Then niy hon. friend says that this is subsequent equipment, and is not covered by the mortgage. It is covered by the mortgage under section 35. _ Therefore, my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) meets the same difficulty under section 35 that he met under my construction, because if you are to have a first charge upon the first equipment, you -must also have a first charge upon the subsequent equipment, and yet, according to the argument of the Minister of Justice, that subsequent equipment need not be vested in the company by an absolute title. If that is not acquired by an absolute title, you cannot give to the words ' first mortgage ' in section 35 the office my hon. friend assigns to them. It is all covered by the same provision :
A mortgage which shall be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property, tolls, rights and franchises of the company, including all equipment and property to be thereafter acquired by the company.
Well, then, the argument of the Minister of Justice, it seems to me, fails when he endeavours to draw the distinction he has drawn. He says that the provision in section 14 refers to subsequent equipment and that subsequent equipment might be acquired under a hiring agreement. If it does, and you rely on section 35, you are up against the same wail as before, because section 30. according to the Minister of Justice, means a first charge upon an absolute title. That charge is to cover not only the first but also subsequent equipment. Then the words in section 35 cannot mean what my hon. friend the Minister of Justice says they mean because he has admitted that the subsequent equipment at least might be acquired by the company under a hiring agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I used the word ' part.' I dad not want to eliminate the word ' part from section 14. I want to insist on giving it effect as on giving effect to everything else. Part of the equipment may be leased, but I put the question seriously to the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) if he believes that, taking section 35 as it is there, if the company acquires property under leasehold interest, the company can give a mortgage on that property which shall be a first charge upon it. If that is the contention, then I cannot understand the meaning of the word.
Li. BORDEN. I have already said that section 35 must be construed in connection with section 14.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
And I have said that the opinion which he has given to this House has absolutely ignored section 14. The Minister of Justice has not ignored it, because he has given a certain office to the words of section 14 and he points out, and is right in pointing out, that section 14 refers in express terms to only part of the equipment. Does the hon. the Minister of Justice get much consolation out of that ? Ninety-nine one hundredths of the equipment would be part of the equipment. There is not much virtue in the word ' part.' Then he says one thing further. He says that those words do not include the first equipment of the road, they include subsequent or additional equipment. I point out to the Minister of Justice that he is in exactly the same difficulty about that under section 35 as if he adopted the construction I have put forward. He asks me:	Do you say
a first charge can be a first charge upon anything but an absolute Interest ? I say that if you take these two sections together vou may have a great deal of doubt about it, because if you find in one section of the sta-

tute that a company Is authorized to equip its road by rolling stock acquired under a title which is not an absolute title, and if you find in another section that the company is to give a mortgage, which shall be a first charge, it is a very fair argument to make, and would he a fair argument to make in any court, that the mortgage which is to be a first charge is to he a first charge upon the interest of the company described in a preceding clause of the contract. Taking those two sections together, it is to be a first charge, not necessarily upon an absolute interest, but a first charge upon the interest which has been described in a preceding clause. That may not be an unanswerable argument. I am not putting it forward as an unanswerable argument, but as an argument which can be reasonably made upon these two sections of the contract, and I must say that, with all due deference to the opinion of the Minister of Justice, I am not at all convinced that it is, not a proper argument and a proper conclusion to be drawn from a consideration and construction of these two sections.

House in committee on Bill (No. 72) to amend the National Transcontinental Railway Act.-Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
On section 1,

Mr. Chairman, before six o'clock the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) referred to a remark that I had made in discussing the mortgage provisions and he stated that the provisions I had referred to in clause 13 of the charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company were not applicable to the mortgage referred to in clause 35 (c) of the original contract. I desire to refer once more to clause 35; it contains this provision :
For the purposes hereinafter in this paragraph respectively defined, the company may and shall create mortgages to trustees, as follows.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Then follow sub-clauses (a), (b) and (c).
(a)	Is an agreement to give a ' first charge ' on certain property, including rolling stock equipment, to secure the bonds guaranteed by the government.
(b)	To give a ' second charge ' on the same property, excepting Eastern Division equipment, to secure bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Company.
(c)	To give a charge upon the Eastern Division equipment, ' next after ' the mortgage or charge (a), to secure the conditions of the lease.
You will observer Mr. Chairman, that (a) is an agreement to create a first mortgage or charge, to secure certain bonds of the company. The power of the company to give such a mortgage is derived from, section 13 of its charter, which section is to be read in connection with section 94 of the general Railway Act 1888, and the mortgage, although called a first mortgage is expressly declared to be subject to the working expenditure of the railway, and working expenditure is declared to include rent of rolling stock. So, Sir, not only is (c), but (a) also is subject to such rentals. Mortgage (c) which is supposed to secure the conditions of the lease is not in any sense whatever a first mortgage. It is expressly made subject to (a) and both are subject to the rolling stock rentals. So that it seems to me that there is very strong ground indeed for contending-I will not say, having respect for the hon. Minister's opinion, that it is absolutely beyond question-that all these mortgages are subject to the working expenditure; in other words, subject to rent of rolling stock. The question is very important, because, as I have pointed out before, if they are subject to the rent of the rolling stock it means that the mortgages of these trustees created under section 35 are subject to a prior lien of 820,000,000. Now, I repeat that even if we were to accept as probable the interpretation put upon this clause by the hon. Minister of Justice it would be a monstrous piece of carelessness on the part of this parliament to have that exposed to litigation, subject to discussion when we have the power to avoid that by simply saying in this Bill now before us that the rolling stock to be provided must be provided free from any lien. The hon. gentleman says that is the intention. I think every hon. gentleman who has spoken on the other side of the House has contended that it is the intention of the government that $20,000,000 of the rolling stock to be provided as equipment shall be absolutely free from any charge for interest, rent or any other claim whatever.
Assuming that is the bargain between the country and the Grand Trunk, where is the harm of saying that it is the bargain ? Sir Rivers-Wilson says he has a different view of it. and the government tell us they do not care what Sir Rivers-Wilson says, that this rolling stock must be clear from every claim

*whatever so that the government shall have a mortgage on the absolute title of ownership in that property. Well, where is the harm of saying so ? Are we to leave it open to those with whom we are contracting to argue that such is not the contract at all ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They do say so.

They do, but let us provide that they cannot say so. One of the most absolute securities that can be created *on a railway property is the rolling stock rental because it goes in with the wages of the workmen and must be paid before anything is given to the creditors; and here is a question whether rent on this $20,000,000 is to become part of the working expenses, and when we ask the government to put it beyond doubt that the rolling stock shall be [DOT]owned, they say they will not do it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have listened to the argument of my hon. friends ojjpo-site, and their contention is that while we put one interpretation on this contract, the president of the Grand Trunk Railway puts another interpretation upon it. As I understand, my hon. friends rely on the statement of Sir Rivers-Wilson-I have not the exact words before me-which if I remember aright was, that it was intended to have the equipment provided by a trust company.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No ; here are his words.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is what the president of the Grand Trunk Railway said :
That rolling stock will be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific, and as the general manager will perhaps tell you, they have laid their plans for providing that rolling stock by a trust fund.
That is the statement made by the president.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He referred to the general manager, and as I understand, the general manager never said a word about it, and that being so you cannot take from the words of the president the meaning that my hon. friends opposite attach to them.

The Prime Minister is not Tight in that contention surely, because the piesident of the Grand Trunk Railway in defining the liabilities of his company direct and indirect, distinctly states that the general manager would say that this large sum was to be provided by a trust fund. It is quite natural that if no further questions were asked, the general manager would not refer to it again, but certainly the president of the company did not refer to that very important matter in these words without having an understanding with the general manager as to how that money was to be
raised. The shareholders took the statement of the president as a matter of course.

Surely the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, whose name is first signed on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific, could speak with as much authority as the general manager, and he says :
That rolling stock will be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and as the general manager will tell you, they have laid their plans to provide that rolling stock by a trust fund. Therefore you may wipe it out-and call it four millions.
It Is true he speaks of a future reference to be made by the general manager, which the general manager does not make, but the president of the company does not the less definitely make the statement. We have been told by the Minister of Customs, and by the Finance Minister, that all these amendments were made simply because the Grand Trunk Railway refused to go on without them. Suppose the Grand Trunk Railway Company should say to-morrow : This is our interpretation of the contract, and unless you construe the contract as we do we shall not proceed further with the enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They would lose their five millions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
If the government should give the same answer as they have given in the past, they would say : interpret the contract as you like ; we will accept your Interpretation of it. The Minister of Justice distinctly took the ground that although my argument might be correct, that the words in section 14 could be construed as relating to the rolling stock equipment of the eastern division ; nevertheless my argument was of no importance because these words referred only to that portion of the rolling stock which should be acquired afterwards ; and he said that so far as the first equipment was concerned that was controlled by paragraph 35 of the original contract under which a mortgage must be given which should be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property. As I pointed out to the Minister of Justice before six o'clock : when he adopted that argument he went too far, because he brings himself up against the fact that in section 35, upon which he relies, the provision is for a mortgage which shall be a first charge not only upon the first equipment, but upon all subsequent equipments.
Therefore the construction of the hon. Minister of Justice is not consistent with the argument he is adopting ; it is absolutely inconsistent with it, because that subsequent rolling stock equipment which he admits1 might be acquired under a hiring agreement is also to be subject to a first charge as much as the first equipment under

the terms of section 35. He is in a worse position after making that argument than he was before, because he has admitted a construction of paragraph 14 which is absolutely inconsistent with the view of this contract which he has expressed to the House. Under these circumstances, as this involves a question of 820,000,000, we are entitled to have put into this contract words which will remove any possible doubt on this question ; and I for my part cannot understand the hesitation of the government, if they are sincere-and we are bound to assume that they are-in the view they are pressing on the committee, I cannot understand their hesitation to accept this amendment and thus put the matter beyond doubt. We are not asking from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company anything beyond what the government themselves say is the-correct interpretation of the contract. Then why hesitate ? We have the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway stating, by necessary implication, if not by express words, that that is not his interpretation of it, and we have offered some argument from this side of the House to show that there may be some foundation for his opinion ; and when we simply ask the government to place the question beyond doubt, there is some extraordinary, unnecessary and unusual hesitation about making the matter plain. Why should it not be made plain ? My right hon. friend, twenty years ago, in discussing the loaning of $30,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, said the government of the day had created a power which was stronger than itself. Has this government created a power which is stronger than itself ? Has it created a power which induces the government to hesitate in placing on the statute book a plain expression setting at rest all possible doubt as to the interpretation of this clause? That is all that is being asked on this side of the House. I for my part cannot understand the hesitation, and I do not think that any other hon. member of this House understands it. If the Grand Trunk Pacific Company understand that contract in the same way as the government understand it, then there ought to be no hesitation on the part of the government in accepting this amendment. On the contrary, if they desire to leave this matter open to doubt, and leave to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company an argument which can be advanced afterwards, and to which the country is to be induced to yield, so that a charge of $20,000,000 is to be placed in priority to this so-called first mortgage-if they desire to leave that open to question, they are adopting the proper means for that purpose. If, however, they desire to safeguard the interests of the country and place this matter beyond question, they are acting in a most extraordinary and unusual manner in opposing this amendment.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Dealing with the argument of the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), I will point out in what respect we differ. He relies on section 13 of the Act of Incorporation as the section which confers on the company the power to issue bonds and give this mortgage, and he says you have to read the last lines of that section which say that the company have a right to create a first charge on the property subject to the provisions contained in section 94 of the Railway Act. My argument is that for the purposes of this agreement we eliminate that section 13 altogether. Section 35 of the agreement contains all the power the company require,, and in that section there is no reference whatever to that reservation in section 13 of the charter. With respect to the question which the hon. leader of the opposition raised, it seems to me you have to give some meaning to the word ' acquired in section 35, and I take issue, straight and direct, with my hon. friend. If I understand him to put it forward as a legal proposition that the company, with a mere leasehold title to this rolling stock, can give to the government the first mortgage contemplated in section 35, then I must differ absolutely from him. You cannot give effect to that clause if you give such a meaning to the word ' acquired.' You can conciliate the terms of section 13 with the terms of section 35. Section 13 applies only to part of the equipment. When you come to section 35, you find that the equipment which the company must put on is an equipment which they must hold by such a title that they can give a mortgage on it which shall be a first mortgage, necessarily exclusive of everything else. If they lease the rolling stock under an arrangement by which, after a certain number of payments are made, the title to the rolling stock passes to the company, it ceases to be held under lease, and becomes absolutely vested in the company, and would be subject to a first mortgage under section 35. It seems to me that you cannot give any effect to that clause unless you put that construction upon it. My hon. friend said a moment ago that we must bear all the clauses in mind. I reply that you must bear in mind not only all the clauses, but all the words of each clause ; and how are you going to give effect to section 35 if you do not interpret it in that way ?
I suppose the Minister of justice will not dispute that a corporation is the creature of its charter. It exists and acts under its charter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend cannot think that I am going to admit that it acts under its charter when it gets subsequent powers under a subsequent Act.

Until a subsequent Act is passed altering its powers under its;

charter it acts under its charter; and in section 13 of its charter this company has power to create first mortgages subject to the provision of section 94 of the General Railway Act of 1888. Section 94 of the Railway Act of 1888 provides that a first mortgage shall be subject to the rental of the rolling stock. There is no question about that, and when a company, created as the Grand Trunk Pacific has been, executes a first mortgage upon al'l its property, you must go back to that section of the Railway Act, and you will there find that that first mortgage is subject to the rent of the rolling stock, that rental being considered part of the work expenditure. 1 now come to what the hon. minister tells us alters all that. The Grand Trunk Pacific enters into a contract with the government, and it is that agreement we are considering now. And what is that company bound to do? Under subsection ' a ' of section 35, it has to give a first mortgage upon its ' undertaking, equipment and property, tolls, rights and franchises, including all equipment and property to be thereafter acquired by the company.' That is perfectly clear. Is not that in accord with section 13? It expressly provides for a mortgage to secure the bonds of the company, which is the very thing that section 13 enables the company to give. The hon. gentleman will not dispute that so far.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is all very technical and very fine.

It is not at all technical, and does not require a very expert lawyer to understand it. Section 13 enables the company to give a first mortgage. The company enters into an agreement with the government to give such a mortgage.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: What is the use of refining in that way when my hon. friend has before him section 2 of the Act authorizing the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, which specially empowers the company to do all that the agreement requires it to do ?

I suppose that this agreement will be construed according to the powers of the company at the time the company entered into it. This company has the power to grant a first mortgage upon all its property, under an Act which says that the first mortgage shall be subject to the rent of the rolling stock. It is empowered by subsection * a ' of section 35 to give a first mortgage to secure the bonds guaranteed by the government. I will drop ' b ' for the present and see what subsection ' c ' says. Subsection 1 c ' provides for a mortgage to secure the conditions of the lease. It reads as follows :
A mortgage which shall be a charge upon the rolling stock constituting the equipment of the eastern division next after the charge mentioned in paragraph 35 (a).
But if the mortgage in paragraph 35 (a) is subject to the rent of the rolling stock, surely the mortgage 'c,' which is subject to paragraph 'a,' must also be subject to the rent of the rolling stock. You cannot make the mortgage in ' c ' a better mortgage than that provided in ' a when ' c ' is subject to * a.' If paragraph ' a ' stood alone, I doubt whether the Minister of Justice would have argued that mortgage * a ' was not subject to the working expense of the railway, and when he takes a mortgage which is subject to ' a ', how can that be in any sense prior to the working expenditure ? If ' a ' is subject to the working expenditures, surely ' c,' which is in a lower grade still, must also be subject to the same expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not believe that the company is the creature of this charter. In my judgment it is the creature of the law which gave it existence. In this respect, without any reference whatever to the charter, suppose that section 13 never existed, under section 35 of the agreement, and section 2 of the National Transcontinental Railway Act, and give it the authority to do that which is necessary to give effect to section 35.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does my hon. friend say that you are not to consider section 35 in conjunction with the terms of the charter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the terms of the charter are amended, you take the amending Act.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do you not have to look at it to see that it is amended ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is amended.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Do you not have to construe the two together ? It is a remarkably novel proposition that you are to deal with this section apart from the charter as the Minister of Justice seems to suggest. You must look at section 35. You must also look at the terms of the charter and the powers conferred by them on the company and construe them in connection with this Act as if they were one Act. That is the view 1 take of the situation as far as the statutes are concerned. The whole point of the argument of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice, with respect to section 14, in answer to myself, turns on one narrow suggestion which he made. He says that the company may make a contract for the hiring of rolling stock, the ownership of -which, after a certain time, will vest in the lessee or the person to whom it is hired. Then he says that after this transfer takes place, the company to whom the rolling stock was so hired will have a good title as owner and then section 35 will have effect. But does my hon. friend say that section 14 is restricted to any such hiring ? If' so, I invite him to show me one word or line which so restricts it. I have made some in-

quiry, and X find that there is not only the method of hiring rolling stock to which my hon. friend has referred, but that there is also a very large business carried on by more than one company-certainly by one very large company-under which the title to the rolling stock is retained for ever in the company which owned it in the first instance, and the payments are perpetual payments, and the rolling stock does not at any time become vested in the person to whom it is hired. Section 14 permits part of the equipment of the eastern division to be so provided, in which case the rolling stock would never vest in the Grand Trunk Pacific. And since section 14 permits that, the argument of the Minister of Justice, based upon the suggestion he made a moment ago, seems to me to absolutely disappear. If he says it does not. I take issue with him just as strongly as he does with me with regard to the legal construction of this contract. I am equally entitled to my opinion as my hon. friend is to his, and I say that construing section 35 with section 14, it seems to me, not only open to reasonable but to convincing argument, that, so far as a part of the equipment of the eastern division is concerned, the Grand Trunk Pacific need not be vested with an absolute and complete title, but will satisfy the conditions of this contract by furnishing a portion of the equipment under an agreement of lease and hire. That is my conviction, after having listened with every respect and attention to what has been said by the Minister of Justice and the First Minister. Under these circumstances, I see no possible reason why this government should be afraid to place upon the terms of the statute a clause which will remove absolutely any doubt, and make the interpretation, which the government says is a true interpretation of this contract, plain beyond doubt and cavil.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would like to put on ' Hansard ' the exact words used by Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, and thus possibly remove some doubts which appear to exist in the minds of some hon. gentlemen.
What is the hon. gentleman reading from ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: From the official report of proceedings at the ordinary general meeting of the company-that is the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada-held at the City Terminus Hotel, Cannon street, London, on Tuesday, 8th March, 1904.
Would there be any difficulty in the way of laying that document on the table and having it printed ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not control the document, nor have I any supply of them.
But could it not be laid on the table ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Mr'. FITZPATRICK. I rose to accomplish a purpose and would like to be allowed to do so. Here is what the president said :
As regards the 5 millions for rolling stock-in the first place the estimate is not 5 millions, hut 3 millions. With that the Grand Trunk Company has nothing to do,
I do not think that anybody would contend that the Grand Trunk had anything to do with the rolling stock. The providing of the rolling stock is an obligation on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific.
That rolling stock will be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and, as the general manager will perhaps tell you, they have laid their plans for providing that rolling stock by a trust fund.
These are the words used as they are reported.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand that the Minister of Justice is reading from a circular to the shareholders dated 28th February ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No ; I am reading from the remarks of the president as reported at the meeting.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fitzpatrick) has been kind enough to send me the document. It is something I had not seen. This is the speech of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: His second speech-after Mr. Allen had spoken.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We have had no correspondence with the president of the Grand Trunk on this point, I think it would not be advisable to have such correspondence. The Grand Trunk Company are aware of the interpretation the government have put on tlie contract. They are aware that we have cited the opinion of the legal gentlemen who framed the contract and have discussed it again and again with then-counsel. This contract was not prepared ex parte by the counsel of the government, but was carefully revised by the counsel of the Grand Trunk and revised jointly by the counsel of the government and the Grand Trunk. It is the matured deliberate opinion of the government. Now, take the words of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson as he uttered them. The most that you could get out of them is simply this,-* That rolling stock will be provided by the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and, as the general manager will perhaps tell you, they have laid their plans for providing that rolling stock by a trust fund.' Let us suppose that Mr. Hays, of the Grand Trunk Pacific, contemplated providing this rolling stock not by the Grand Trunk Pacific or by the Grand Trunk, but by a separate organization. It seems to me clear beyond a doubt that, whoever may be the parties who organize the trust, they must carry on their operations subject to the conditions of the Act which we are nowdiscussing. The conditions upon which they place that rolling stock upon the road- w-hether they take the precaution of ascertaining w-hat the conditions are or not-are those provided by the Act. The Act says that, whoever places this rolling stock upon the road to comply with the conditions of the contract he must place it in such a way
as to give to the government a first mortgage. So, if the rolling stock be provided by a trust, the trust must be ready to take a second mortgage and give the government the first mortgage. That is the argument w-hicli we have from our counsel, and it seems to me it must strike hon. gentlemen on the other side as reasonable. I listened with some care-with great care indeed- to all the arguments addressed to the House from the other side. I do not pretend to discuss the matter after the gentlemen w-ho have given it their best attention and consideration. But, looking at it in the light of ordinary rules of legal interpretation of a contract, one surely must say that these words are as binding as they can be :
For the purposes hereinafter in this paragraph respectively defined, the company may and shall create mortgages to trustees as follows :-
(a.) A mortgage which shall he a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property, tolls, rights and franchis'es of the company.
Now-, it is to be remarked, before we go further, that this Act provides that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company must build a road extending from a certain point to a certain point. Upon that road they must place rolling stock to the amount of $20,000,000. They are not at liberty to'rttSfe-'5ard- any of these provisions. The contract is not completed until they have built the road and put upon it $20,000,000 worth of rolling stock. Then the special Act says explicitly in so many words that upon this there should be a first mortgage. The hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) has drawn an argument also from the words w-hieli follow- :
Including all equipment and property to be thereafter acquired by the company.
Now when they provide rolling stock to the amount of $20.< 00,000 upon w-hich they may be able to give a first mortgage they can obtain rolling stock also upon lease : they can obtain it in full ownership or they can lease it, and it is provided that if they acquire roads these roads shall be subject to the lien of the government, but if they lease roads they cannot give a first mortgage upon them. Therefore, upon this it seems to me that the amendment is very clear, that anything they acquire subsequently comes into the mortgage if they can give a first mortgage upon it. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) say : How do you construe this section 14, which contemplates that rolling stock may be hired. Rolling stock may be hired and certainly the drafters of this Act never contemplated that the Grand Trunk Pacific would have to put only $20,000,000 w-ortli of rolling stock on the road. They contemplated that the Grand Trunk, as the enterprise developed, would be forced to put on more than $20,000,000

worth and they gave the company the latitude to lease rolling stock as well as to buy and purchase it. There is nothing extraordinary in that and they contemplated that probably it would be better for them to lease than to purchase it, and therefore they provided that if any part of it was leased beyond $20,000,000 under such circumstances the hire could go as part of the expenditure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is there in section 14 that enacts that the hiring of equipment is to be restricted to that which is subsequently hired ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The contract contemplates that there shall be acquired $20,000,000 worth of rolling stock upon which a first mortgage can be given. Then I say that as far as this $20,000,000 is concerned, it is impossible to conceive that they can lease it. They must give a first mortgage upon it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What are the words in section 14 that enact that ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The words are to be found in section 35. My hon. friend has said again and again that the contract is not to be interpreted as so many separate clauses, but that all the clauses must be contemplated. Taking section 14 and section 35 together it seems to me that you have it beyond a doubt that to the extent of $20,000.000 the company must give a first mortgage. If the company leases the rolling stock upon which they give that mortgage it does not fulfil the contract. If the company having purchased $20,000,000 of stock, leases $5,000,000 worth more of stock they are within their rights beyond a doubt. Under such circunflstances you come under the terms of section 14 and the hiring of this rolling stock would be counted as expenditure. My hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) says why do you not agree to this, or to this. I may say that more precautions have been taken upon this contract than have ever before been taken on any contract of the kind. We have had the best legal advice we could obtain not only to interpret the contract but to prepare and to draft it. When the best counsel tell us that this is the construction, I think that we can stand by it and ask the House to accept it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am not finding fault with the gentlemen who drafted the contract, but I have to take the contract as I find it and to use my own common sense and experience as best I can in the endeavour to understand what it means. I would like the right hon. gentleman now to follow me attentively, because I want an answer. I asked him to point to me any words in section 14 which indicate that the hiring of rolling stock is confined to that equipment which is subsequently acquired and is not to apply to any portion of the equipment acquired in the first instance. My right hon. friend answered me and said : You Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
must construe section 35 with section 14. And when you come to section 35 you discover there the provision that the company is to give a mortgage which shall be a first charge. Does not my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) realize when he looks at section 35 that that answer will not do ? Surely he must realize that. The Minister of Justice has been struggling with that difficulty and has not been able to overcome it. Section 35 provides for-
A mortgage which shall be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment

That is the first equipment, but there is something else.
-including all equipment and property to be thereafter acquired.
Therefore section 35 puts you exactly iii the same position, as to a'll equipments. There can be no doubt about that. How are you to say that you get any light toy going to section 35 ? Section 14 is not restricted by any words so that it shall mean that rolling stock may be hired for subsequent equipment and shall not be hired for the first equipment. There is no word in section 14 that points to that, not one word from beginning to end, and if yon attempt to construe it by section 35 you are met with exactly the difficulty I have been pointing out, the difficulty that the mortgage on all equipments must be a first mortgage. If my right hon. friend's contention is right it must be a first mortgage not only upon the first equipments tout upon all subsequently acquired equipments. Therefore it does not put these two equipments in contradistinction; it puts them on the same footing and they are left in the same position by the terms of the two clauses. Inasmuch as under paragraph 14 of this agreement you have a distinct l'ecognition of the right of the company to furnish some portion of its equipment by means of a hiring agreement and as under paragraph 35 you have no distinctions between the first equipments and subsequent equipments so far as the character of the title is concerned, then you are at once forced to a conclusion that this company, whether the first equipment or a subsequent equipment is in question, is at liberty to furnish some portion of that equipment by means of a hiring agreement. That is the inevitable conclusion to which we are driven and I must say that I have not got much light thereon from my hon. friends, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. and of course I say that with all respect to their arguments. I am saying that in all sincerity and I am stating what I believe to be the true Interpretation of the contract.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I also am giving my own views and I do it also with due deference to the opinions of hon. gentlemen opposite, but I ask the hon. gentleman to again look at section 14. I think he and I agree that section 14 contemplates that for

the equipment of the road rolling stock may be purchased and rolling stock may be leased. That is my view.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There is no question about that ; undoubtedly it may be purchased and we say it may be leased too.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Undoubtedly that is so. Then if we have this much admitted on both sides of the House, let us go beyond that. We next come to section 35. It is admitted on both sides that the rolling stock under section 14 may be leased and it may be purchased. I suppose my hon. friend will agree also that in order to give a first mortgage to the government the rolling stock must be owned by the company. I cannot improve on what I said before but I will try to make my meaning a little clearer. By this contract it is provided that the company undertake to build a railway from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean and they undertake to equip this section as well as the other section to the extent of $20,000,000. Well, how are we to interpret these words ?
A mortgage which shall be a first charge upon the railway, undertaking, equipment and property, toils, rights and franchises of the company.
The only way in which I can interpret that is in order to give effect to the covenant of the company the rolling stock to the extent of $20,000,000 which is to be supplied under the contract by the company must be owned by such a title as will enable them to give a first mortgage upon it. Then, the company may also subsequently and beyond that acquire and purchase rolling stock or other property. Not only can they acquire rolling stock, but they can acquire other railways, branch railways, different roads and everything they subsequently acquire a title to becomes also subject to mortgage to the government. If they do not acquire the title to the property, if they lease it, then of course, the government cannot claim a lien upon that. It seems to me that there is as fair an interpretation of the contract as you can have.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My right hon. friend has made rather an extraordinary argument, because, according to his view, all the company need do in order to avoid giving any mortgage at all is simply to hire this rolling stock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, it cannot escape that.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I understand from the argument of my right hon. friend that if the company wish to avoid giving a mortgage, all they have to do is to hire the rolling stock. At least that is his argument about the subsequently acquired rolling stock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is m.v argument.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, how does he escape the effect of section 14, which makes no distinction in terms between the first acquirement and the subsequent acquirement of rolling stock and I do not see any such distinction by necessary implication. I do not think that the interests of 'the country are very - well protected by the argument which he suggests. My right hon. friend in the first part of his remarks, assumed the very question which we are discussing. He says : They must provide $20,000,000 of rolling stock. We say they must, but the question is : By what title are they to provide it ? How does the contract safeguard the interests of the country in that respect ? What possible effect are you to give to the words in section 14 ? The hire of rolling stock ilet to the company is a part of the working expenditure. Does the section say that that applies to the first equipment or to the subsequent equipment ? It says neither. It may be both. Part of the first equipment and" part of the second equipment may be by means of a hiring agreement. I think further that when you consider section 14, and section 35 together, you have a complete answer to the argument of the hon. Minister of Justice. I say that the expression first mortgage' means a first mortgage upon such title as is contemplated by this agreement. I say it means that and no more. It cannot mean anything more. Then, if by construing section 14 and 35 together, you find that some portion of the equipment (and some portion may mean ninety-nine one-hundredths), can be furnished by a hiring agreement, this provision for equipment, outlined toy the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, can be completely carried out as to that portion. Yet, the government for some reason which I am not sure I can comprehend, declines to remove the doubt, that more than doubt, declines to place upon the statute book a clause which would remove for ever any possible question as to the necessity of the Grand Trvqrk Railway Company acquiring and having an absolutely indefeasible title to that rolling stock.

The hon. Minister of Justice stated before six o'clock that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the government were quite in accord as to this agreement and understood what it meant. The hon. Minister of Justice says that the government understood that this equipment is to be provided and paid for in cash. The president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, the promoter of the Grand Trunk Pacific, states distinctly that the equipment is to be provided by a rolling stock trust. No one who has had the first experience in railway matters could suggest that there could be any two meanings on such a subject. There is only one meaning

when a railway man speaks of creating rolling stock by a trust. That means that the rolling stock is bought by a long hiring lease. There cannot be any other meaning. It is not discussable by any one who knows the first thing about railway matters. The Grand Trunk Railway Company uis-ciaim all liability in connection with the money which is to be provided for this rolling stock. Under the agreement presented to the House all means of credit by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are exhausted by the issue of bonds and the transference of stock to the Grand Trunk Railway Company, so that if it comes to a question of providing the rolling stock by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, they have no means of raising the money to pay for it unless through the endorsation of the Grand Trunk Railway Company or some equally solvent and wealthy concern. There can be no possible question on that subject. I may venture to make the assertion that if this contract goes on and if the government insist upon their interpretation of this clause, we will have another amendment next year, or at some subsequent meeting of this House, to allow the rolling stock to be hired as the Grand Trunk president outlined in his speech that it is intended to be hired. As a layman listening to the discussion and to the expression of the differences of opinion between the legal gentlemen on the other side of the House and the legal gentle-on this side of the House, I think there is not a layman here but feels thgt if this were his own transaction he would not like to put himself into the position of signing this agreement while leaving such an important question undecided. This agreement will be open to dispute from the very fi,rst. The government will state that they understand a clause to mean one thing while the president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company has stated to his shareholders that he takes it to mean another thing. When a condition like that arises and when that condition may be so simply removed by making it plain as to what the meaning is, there must be some.stronger reason than that we have had given to the committee to-day, or on a previQus occasion, when this point was discussed, why the government should refuse to amend that clause so as to make the measure clear beyond dispute as to the meaning in years hereafter. If it is so plain from a legal point of view as interpreted by the Minister o: Justice, I cannot understand why he dees not at once accept the amendment offered by the opposition, and make it so clear that even an ordinary layman can un-clerstand what the contract means.

Statutes are difficult to understand in any case, and it is the duty of the enacting power to make their meaning as clear as possible. We discussed this important question last session, and it was well Mr. OSLER.
known to the Grand Trunk Pacific authorities what the contention of the opposition was upon the question. It was known also what had been said by the government, and in the face of that Sir Rivers-Wilson and the manager of the Grand Trunk Railway interpreted it as having a different meaning from the language of the. amendment. It is said by the Prime Minister that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson having referred to Mr. Hays as endorsing his statement that the rolling stock would be procured by lease and not by purchase, and Mr. Hays not having said anything, that showed that Mr. Hays did not concur in the view taken by Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson. Why, Sir, the very opposite is the fair and logical construction to be placed upon the incident. Silence gives consent, and Mr. Hays, not having disputed the statement of Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, we must infer that Mr. Hays concurred in that satement. I was amazed, and the country will be amazed, to hear the leader of the government advance a proposition so devoid of common sense, if I may be allowed to express myself as I feel. T hope the right hon. gentleman will now amend his views in that regard. Over and over again the ministers have said that our construction of the contract is what is intended. But knowing as they do that the Grand Trunk people have definitely expressed an opposite view, surely it is the duty of the government to accept our amendment and place the matter beyond all doubt. The Minister of Justice attached a good deal of weight to the fact that when the lease came to be executed certain indemnities had to be given. Well, we have nothing more than the covenant of the Grand Trunk Company, without security, that these indemnities will be forthcoming, and if they are not forthcoming it is left for us to sue the company. If the government be sincere in their desire to protect the public, as we must suppose they are, there is no reason in the world why they should not accept this amendment. It is not now a question of leaving this Act intact as it was introduced to this House. Hon. gentlemen will remember that in the earlier stages of this discussion the Minister of Justice told us that this Bill was drawn with very great care, and that he hesitated to have any alteration made. That plea does not avail the government to-night, for not only are numerous amendments proposed by the Minister of Justice himself, but in several instances amendments suggested by this side of the House are being made for the purpose of clearing up the meaning. When the Minister of Justice is altering the Act in some particulars in order to make it more clear, surely it is the duty of the government to make its meaning clear in this very important particular.

It has always been surprising to me, a layman, that there is so

298t>
often such diversity of opinion amongst lawyers in the interpretation of a law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And doctors do not differ.

Doctors may differ, hut we always aim at coming to an understanding so as to remove diversity of opinion. It has always seemed to me that where we are legislating on contracts such language should he used as would be absolutely clear and capable of no interpretation but the one which we intend. This contract involves an immense sum of money, but lawyers on that side differ from lawyers on this side as to its proper interpretation, and even the Minister of Justice must have some doubt, because he submitted this very clause for the opinion of a firm of lawyers in Toronto. The object of the amendment moved from this side of the House is to put the meaning of the clause beyond all question of doubt, and surely, for the purpose of clearness and for the purpose of safeguarding the interests of the country, the government ought to accept our proposition.
It seems to me that you could hardly use the English language in any way that would make the matter plainer or more conclusive than it is made in the amendment.
