We find that the Grand Trunk Railway is given the right to lease any portion of the road pending the completion of the whole
line, but we do not find that the government have any corresponding right to compel the Grand Trunk Railway to take out a lease. The whole thing is one-sided. For instance, it is provided that a lease of the portion must not be more onerous than the terms of the lease of the whole, but they may be as much less onerous as the commissioners may see fit. It was not at all necessary for the government to provide that a lease of any portion of the line should not be less onerous than the lease in the original agreement, but it was considered necessary to protect the company by providing that it could not be more onerous. As I understand this matter, there is no room for argument as to what the new terms mean. We have in the original lease a provision that for seven years the company is not to pay any rent and for the following three years the company may have the road without paying anything, and the rental for the three years is then to be capitalized at three per cent.
Well, this new lease, if the commissioners execute it, is to be on terms not more onerous than the other. That is, if it is for seven years it will be without rent. I ask, is that fair and reasonable, having regard to existing conditions, as placed before the House ? We have, for instance, a description by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) last session when the original contract was under consideration. Another phase of the question was being argued, and it was to the Minister of the Interior's interest, as he conceived it, to contrast this scheme with the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and he said :
I want to say a word or two in regard to the prospects of this enterprise from a financial standpoint ; and I speak as one who has had a considerable personal knowledge of the development of the western country, and of the differences that have been produced in the financial conditions of the railway companies owing to that development. The net profits of the Canadian Pacific Railway during the year ending the 30th of June, 1902, were $14,085,000, and last year its net profits were $15,000,000. The company have made of their railway enterprise a magnificent success, and if they were called upon to-morrow to incur the liability to pay back every cent of public subvention which they have received, and all the money which they have received for iands, notwithstanding that, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would be a good, sound and solvent concern.
What does that mean ? It means this, as I understand it-that if you take every dollar of assistance from the Grand Trunk Pacific and let them build a road from North Bay to the Pacific coast without any subvention at all, it will be a good, sound, solvent, paying concern. I shall not proceed further to emphasize the contrast which the minister makes, showing how vastly superior he claims this enterprise is under the conditions which surround it to the Canadian Pacific Railway-and, as is remarked to me by an hon. friend, the aid to

ready referred should be rejected by the government. I do not think that anything can be said in favour of it which has not already been said in respect to the other and therefore I will content myself with moving it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I understand that the argument here would be absolutely the same as that in respect of the other amend: ment respecting the rolling stock so we can take it that what was said on the other on both sides is said on this.
Amendment (Mr. R. L. Borden) negatived.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
There is another amendment which has been suggested to section 1. My hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) will move it, but preparatory to his moving it I will say a few words about it. The amendment is as follows :
That all freight originating on the line of the Pacific Company's railway or upon the branch lines, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, where destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports, and that the rates for such carriage shall not be greater than the rates charged between the same points over any route not wholly Canadian which includes any part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company system.
The first branch of this is already covered by section 42 of the contract, which is simply repeated as introductory to the second part, which is as follows :
That the rates for such carriage shall not be greater than the rates charged between the same points over any route not wholly Canadian which includes any part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company system.
It is possible that the Grand Trunk Railway Company may have an all-Canadian route from Winnipeg to Montreal and that they may have a route from Winnipeg to Montreal which is not wholly Canadian and which embraces some portion of the system of the Grand Trunk Railway Company in the United States. The object of the amendment is to provide that the rates for such carriage shall not be greater by the Canadian route than the rates charged between the same points by a route not wholly Canadian, which includes any part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company's system. The reason for the amendment seems to be quite obvious and I have stated it thus briefly. My hon. friend who is to move the amendment, will, I have no doubt, give such further explanations as he deems necessary.

It seems to me that after the very lucid statement made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition as to the object of this amendment, I need not take up the time of the committee at any great length in explaining it. Section 42 of the agreement of last year declares the conditions upon which aid was given to the Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
Grand Trunk Pacific. That section states that:
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and -the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.
The company accept the aid on the conditions which I have here before me and which I have just recited.
The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of the railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian (territory, o'r' between Canadian inland ports.
So far so good. Then the company obligates itself in the concluding sentence of section 42 that:
The through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports than via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
I take it that this clause means that traffic originating in Winnipeg or any point in the west destined for Liverpool or any point across the ocean shall not be carried by the Grand Trunk via United States ports at a through rate less than would be given on the same class of goods if carried via Canadian ports to their destination. But there is no provision made against a discrimination of rates in regard to interprovincial traffic which may go over the new line. The object of the government in giving this aid as stated in the first part of section 42 is this :
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels.
I opine that interprovincial trade will for many years to come be the great bulk of the trade which will be likely to be carried over this new road and it is eminently essential, as we desire this trade for this route, that there shall be no discrimination in rates. The object of the amendment is to prevent such discrimination and to provide that between such points as have already been mentioned by my hon. frieud the leader of the opposition there shall be no discrimination. It is to provide that if a consignment of freight is earied from Winnipeg to Hamilton, or Toronto, or Montreal over the all-rail Canadian route, the rate shall not be any greater than via Duluth and Chicago and thence to its destination at Hamilton, or Toronto, or Montreal. It seems

*to me that the reasonableness of this amendment must be apparent to hon. gentlemen opposite. I take it that it was an oversight in the drafting of the clause that this provision was not placed in the contract. The amendment deals, I say, with rates on interprovincial traffic. The section of last year only made provision against discrimination on through traffic destined for export. Internal traffic should be treated on the same favourable conditions as export traffic and the amendment which is now before me makes that provision. I think hon. gentlemen will see the propriety and reasonableness of accepting this amendment, because if it is accepted it will certainly promote the object which hon. gentlemen had in view ' in giving such enormous aid to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, as it will promote the carriage of Canadian goods by Canadian routes. I do not thiDk that I need take up the time of the committee in elaborating that point at any greater length.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The answer to this from the point of view of the government is that in regard to interprovincial traffic we have, under the Railway Commission, absolute and unlimited control of rates. We would not1 have that absolute and unlimited control of rates on export traffic because the through rate includes not only the rail rate but the ocean rate. On grain business, which is chiefly in mind,1 there is usually a through rate which is quoted say from Winnipeg to Liverpool. That wohld not be under the control of the Railway Commission because it would include the water rate. But, that would not apply to interprovincial traffic. Interprovincial traffic is without any limitation subject to the provisions of the Railway Act and the Railway Commissioners can meet any such difficulty as that which my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) suggests. If it be found that there is an attempt to resort to unfair discrimination *as respects interprovincial traffic there is under the Railway Act the most full and ample machinery for protecting the public interest. This company is not the only one which might have connections through the United States and although I have not thought of that aspect of it so much, I think there might be something said to the effect that if any such provision is necessary it should apply to all railways and not to this one only. There would be no particular reason why one company should be discriminated against because they may have done this while another company would be permitted to do precisely the same thing. But, the chief ground we take is that as respects interprovincial traffic the provisions of the Railway Act give ample protection to the public interest.
Do I understand my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Field-irg) to say that the board of Railway Commissioners can control rates by way of Chicago ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, but they can control rates over this road, and if it can be shown that this company by any roundabout way is giving more favourable rates otherwise, then the railway commissioners can insist that the Canadian rates shall be reduced.

What we say, is that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should be a party to this arrangement in controlling the Grand Trunk Pacific and if the Grand Trunk Railway by its Chicago route makes a rate between Winnipeg and Toronto, it ought to give as good a rate by the all-Canadian route between the same points. Why should the Grand Trunk, receiving all these benefits, be permitted to be a party to a lower rate by a route of which it forms a part through tiie United States, than it gives through Canada ? There may be a question as to whether the Grand Trunk might not reasonably object to be bound to compete with rates by any and every line in the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Why not ?

For the reason that no corporation wants to be bound to any rate which another rival company may make. You could compel the Grand Trunk to meet a rate which it joined in making through the United States, but it might be a different thing if some other company were, for the purpose of hurting the Grand Trunk, to make a very low rate, in order to compel the Grand Trunk to follow it. There cannot be any objection to compelling the Grand Trunk to give the same rate to the all-Canadian route, that it joins with other companies in allowing by the United States route.

The Grand Trunk Railway accepts the aid upon the conditions stated in section 42 ; that it is for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade by the transportation of goods through Canadian channels, and it also agrees that all freight originating on the line of railway or its branches not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall when destined for points in Canada be carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports. The amendment proposes that there should be no descri-minating rate so far as the Grand Trunk Railway are concerned against the all-Canadian route as between points in Canada. Admitting all the Finance Minister has said as to the powers of the Railway Commission, would it not be much simpler that there should be a distinct statement made in this agreement that the Grand Trunk shall not be a party to making any discriminating rates against the all-Canadian route ? If the Grand Trunk Railway have entered into this contract in good faith and desire to
son

implement the intention of the government to develop Canadian trade in Canadian channels, surely it is not an unreasonable request that they shall not discriminate in the rates to be charged as between points in western Canada and eastern Canada ?
Ma FIELDING;. Last year my hon. friends did not value that clause as highly as they do now.
I moved this amendment last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken. What is proposed now is, that the clause of our original contract which has reference in part to inland traffic and in part to ocean traffic, shall now be specifically adapted to the inland traffic, and in their amendment they quote almost the very words of that poor despised and miserable clause which we proposed a year ago, and they take it as the chief corner stone of their argument.
I moved the same amendment last year, and the hon. gentleman voted it down.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite agree that when the Grand Trunk Pacific Company accepts the aid as set forth in this contract for the specific purpose of encouraging trade through Canadian channels, then if they did that which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) says they would do
I did not say they would do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said they might do it, and if there was not a possibility of their doing it the amendment is of no use. I quite agree that the doing of that thing would be a direct breach of that contract. I, as a layman, would not hesitate to say that it would be a gross breach of the whole spirit of the contract, and that being the case, the Railway Commission would not for a moment permit the Grand Trunk Pacific to do it. What my hon. friend desires to accomplish by his amendment is already provided for " most adequately by the Act constituting the Railway Commission.
Would the Minister of Justice
Oh, oh.
If hon. gentlemen try to adopt these tactics they will not succeed.
Oh.
Some of these gentlemen think they are so exceedingly clever.
Hear, hear. Oh.
They think they can give impertinence to members who are addressing the House. I know when to speak and when to be silent, and I do not get up for the purpose of talking.
Oh.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I get up to speak on something I know something about, and when hon. gentlemen have been outside and come into the chamber they should be quiet.
Oh, oh.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I ask you to keep order. The Minister of Justice said that this matter would be controlled by the Railway Commission. Let me point out that when specific provisions are made in this contract, the Railway Commission would be very liable to say that parliament having made special provisions it would not be proper for them to interfere. The Railway Act expressly provides that it does not interfere wTith any special legislation affecting any railway company, and here we have special legislation affecting this particular matter. It is questionable if the Railway Commission would interfere and we certainly should not leave the matter in this condition of doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is some special legislation on this subject, but unfortunately for the gentleman's argument it is special legislation the other way. It is special legislation in the contract of last year ratified by this House, and section 39 says :
The rates and toils to be levied and taken by the company upon any part of the said railway, shall be 'under the control of the Governor in Council, or of such authority, commission, or tribunal, as is designated or constituted under any Act of the parliament of Canada, for the regulation or control of the business of railways.
Therefore the matter is dealt with, not only by the general provisions of the Railway Act, but by the specific terms of the contract of last year.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is that not rather an argument against the Minister of Finance than for him ? A little while ago he was suggesting that there should be no special provision, because all the necessary provisions were contained in the General Act. The same argument would eliminate from the agreement section 39, which he has just referred to. What is the office of that section if his argument of a moment ago was a valid one ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Because when that Clause was drawn there was no railway commission, and the section of the contract provides for the Railway Commission which was in contemplation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Does my hon. friend remember that the Act constituting the Railway Commission is declared to be a substitution for the former Railway Act, and the tribunal thex-eby created is declared to be a continuation of the former Railway Committee ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: With powers a hundred per cent greater.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Quite so, but the Act, applies in general terms to every railway in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Railway Commission will not apply to a government owned road.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This is not a govern ment owned road.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Of course it is.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: A large part of it is not. It is a government owned road as to the eastern division, but operated by a company.	-

While this section provides that the rates shall be under the control of the Governor in Council, it does not provide that they can reduce rates. The provisions of the Crow's Nest Pass Bill were entirely different from this. That Bill not only put the rates under the control of the Governor in Council, but gave it power to reduce the rates. Under the old law the tolls were practically under the control of the Governor in Council, because if it did not consent to them, no railway company could charge them ; but it has always been contended that that did not give the Governor in Council the right to reduce the tolls. If that be so, under the present law, which I think has the same words, the Governor in Council could not compel a railway company to lower its tolls, though they might be too high. Therefore, it seems to me that it would be necessary to have some such provision as was put in the Crow's Nest Pass Bill to give the Governor in Council power to lower the tolls at any time if it thought them too high.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I suppose what my hon. friend refers to is the rule that where a maximum rate was fixed the companies were free to charge up to that amount. Of course, the Governor in Council could reduce the rates by fixing a lower maximum. Under the new Railway Act it is different. The Railway Commission does not fix a maximum tariff, but it can fix the exact rate to be charged on every article, _and nothing can be collected above that. The powers of the Governor in Council were broad before, but the powers of th'e Railway Commission are broader still. The effect of this section 39 is to carry the provisions of the Railway Act into this contract. Even without it, the provisions of the general law would apply, but we are making assurance doubly sure.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Is not that a good argument for carrying this into the special Act, instead of leaving it to the operations of the general law ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we undertook to change this contract, it would be necessary to have a meeting of the shareholders of the
Grand Trunk Company to ratify the change. Therefore, we say that unless it is necessary to make a change of great importance, we would not be justified in imperilling the whole contract by making changes. Everything the hon. gentleman asks is accomplished by general legislation in the strongest and fullest terms.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is very frank on the part of my hon. friend. The situation appears to be that if the government had thought of it they would have put a clause in here similar to section 39 ; but, as they did not think of it, they do not do it, because, if they did it, it might result in some difficulty with the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
The Minister of Justice said some of the clauses were improperly drawn and must be drawn over again. How is it he could change those clauses ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Justice did not speak of any change in the contract, but in the clauses of the Bill. These ^an be amended, and I am sure the Minister of Justice is always glad to accept suggestions ; but he cannot change the contract.

Did I understand the Minister of Justice to say that a government owned road does not come under the Railway Act ?
Mr, FITZPATRICK. The Railway Act does not apply to a government owned road ; but in order to set all questions at rest with regard to this railway, it is provided that the tolls and charges on the eastern division shall be subject to the approval of the Railway Commission.

In settling rates for Canada the Board of Railway Commissioners will have regard for what may be a reasonable rate to impose upon the railway company. But at times rates may be allowed via Chicago lower than the commissioners would impose on the Canadian route. The effect would be that traffic would be diverted from the Canadian line. Now, what we say is, that if the Grand Trunk join in any such low rate via Chicago it must give as good a rate through Canada even though lower than our commissioners impose. We say that that should be made a matter of contract here in consideration of the aid we are giving. The resolution we are moving now is almost in the very words of the resolution moved last year by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) to be found at page 12751 of ' Hansard ' :
That all freight originating on the line of the said railway or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, if destined for points in Canada, shall he carried entirely on Canadian territory or between Canadian inland ports, and that the rates for such carriage shall not be greater than the rate charged between the same points by any route not wholly

Canadian, and if any such freight be for export, it shall-
Then it goes on with the rest of the-clause as in section 42 of the agreement. I understood the hon. Minister of Finance to rather plume himself on having found something good in the contract of last year which we opposed. That is the amendment we moved last yea r, upon which the one we are now discussing is based.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whether it was moved by the hon. gentleman himself or by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), the words were largely those in the clause of the original contract, and when that clause was brought up in its application to export traffic, my hon. friend and others argued that it did not amount to anything. Of course, if hon. gentlemen were glad to take it at the latter part of last session or if they desire to take it now, we are pleased to know that our efforts in that direction are appreciated.

The object of our amendment last year was to insert the words which my hon. friend from West Toronto is now moving to have inserted. We did not propose to strike out clause 42 of the agreement, but we pointed out where it was defective. As the hon. member for West Toronto has said, the government apparently overlooked the necessity of providing for rates on the inland traffic from point to point within Canada. My hon. friend from West Toronto is now moving to have a clause inserted similar to the one we proposed last year. The object of our motion last year was to make the hon. gentleman's clause effective.
Amendment negatived.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall section 1 be adopted ?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: There are some of these amendments which are not strictly speaking amendments to any special clause of the Bill. It may be convenient to introduce them between the various clauses or at the end.

speechtext:
I understood the arrangement to be that my hon. friend would be free to introduce them at any time he thought proper.
